docs.title: Mujou
docs.text:
Asynchronous Distributed Deep Learning Library for Continuous Learning

Image: a new work based on Yoichi Ochiai's Liquid Universe.

Mujou is a deep learning framework in which a network of connected nodes keeps inferring and learning at the same time.

Early development

Mujou is in an early stage of development. The API may change without notice.

docs.title: A network that keeps learning
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph T["Conventional machine learning"]
        direction LR
        T1["Train (repeat epochs)"] --> T2["Freeze the weights"] --> T3["Infer"]
    end
    subgraph M["Mujou"]
        direction LR
        M1["Input"] --> M2["Network (infers and learns at once)"] --> M3["Output"]
        M2 -->|"weights keep changing"| M2
    end

The name comes from 無常 (mujō, impermanence: nothing stays the same), as in the Buddhist phrase 諸行無常. Mujou builds machines that keep learning from a stream and keep changing, for uses that learn while they act, such as real-time processing and robotics.

In the program below, a chain of PC-ALM nodes (three of them learning) keeps running while each incoming batch is first predicted and then learned from as a regression (walked through in 5. Learn with PC-ALM).

SHOWN = 0.032  # seconds of the run's timer each batch is shown
# tau.h sets how fast the credit settles (and the period of the nodes, h / 2),
# and the weights learn once per batch, by SGD at the rate
# SHOWN / optimizer.tau = 0.3.
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3)
optimizer = pc.optim.SGD(tau=SHOWN / 0.3)
torch.manual_seed(0)  # the initial weights, before the run
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Linear(64, 1),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 2)),
    y=TensorSpec((B, 1)),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.loss.MSELoss(B),  # the loss of each sample, (B,)
    tau=tau,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    learn_interval=0.75 * SHOWN,  # learn once, 3/4 of the way through each batch
)

torch.set_num_threads(1)
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
every = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)  # every sample has a target, and is new
losses: list[float] = []
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    for i in range(300):
        x = 2 * torch.rand(B, 2, generator=g) - 1
        y = torch.sin(2 * x[:, :1]) * torch.cos(x[:, 1:])
        sample = pc.msg.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=every, reset=every)
        p = pc.show(run, net, sample, seconds=SHOWN)
        losses.append(nn.functional.mse_loss(p["y_hat"], y).item())  # before learning
        if i == 0 or (i + 1) % 50 == 0:
            recent = losses[-50:]
            mean = sum(recent) / len(recent)
            print(
                f"batch {i + 1:3d}: loss {mean:.4f} (the mean of the last {len(recent)})"
            )
    # The state of a node, by its path: input, layer0, layer1, output.
    lam = run.state_dict()["nodes"]["layer0"]["state"]["lam"]
print(f"the mean |lam| of layer0 (its credit) at the end: {lam.abs().mean():.2e}")

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• 🔄 Inference and learning at once: no training mode, no inference mode, no epochs
  • 🧩 Nodes in PyTorch: each node is written and run in PyTorch
  • ⚡ Asynchronous nodes: each node updates on its own schedule and never waits for another
  • ⏱️ Continuous time: nodes update in proportion to dt, the time that really passed
  • 🧠 Any update rule: BP inside a node, PC-ALM across nodes, or a rule of your own
  • 💾 Save the state: take the state of a network and resume from it later
  • 🧪 Simulation and deterministic tests: step virtual time by hand and simulate as fast as the machine computes

docs.title: 📝 Changelog
docs.text: The changes of each release. Until 1.0.0, a minor release (0.x.0) may break the API; a patch release (0.x.y) only fixes bugs. The same notes are on the GitHub Releases.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• mujou.run_manually and mujou.ManualRun at the top level, for simulations: the network runs on virtual time, stepped by hand as fast as the machine computes. run_manually takes workers= as mujou.run does. See the new topic Simulation.
  • pc.Layer(cuda_graph=True): the node records the vector-Jacobian product of its module in a CUDA graph and replays it in every update, the same bit for bit with far fewer kernel launches from the CPU (an update of a ViT stage with one sample: 2.06 ms to 0.47 ms on an RTX 4090).
  • pc.optim.SGD(tau_m=...): SGD with a momentum, the gradient averaged with the time constant tau_m in seconds and corrected for its start at zero by a mass, as in pc.optim.AdamW. It keeps the learning rate: with a constant gradient, the weights move as without the momentum. Without tau_m, pc.optim.SGD is as before.
  • pc.optim.RMSProp(tau=, tau_v=, eps=1e-8): RMSProp in time, the gradient divided by the root of its mean square, which decays with the time constant tau_v in seconds and is corrected by a mass, as in pc.optim.AdamW. It has no momentum and no weight decay.
  • pc.optim.TimeScaled(optimizer, scale=): runs another optimizer on a time scale times as fast, a step of elapsed seconds being one of elapsed * scale seconds of optimizer, so all of its time constants are divided by scale. For one stream shown as batches of scale consecutive samples, with the time constants in the stream's seconds; the relaxation of r and lam is not scaled. See the new section "One stream as a batch of consecutive samples" of the PC-ALM topic.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• ManualRun.step(dt) without nodes updates every node in parallel from the values at the start of the step (Jacobi), instead of one after another in the order of the tree. Pass the nodes (step(dt, *nodes)) to update them in a given order.
  • pc.Layer sends the credit g_in back, and learns, from the delta it has just relaxed in the same update, instead of from the delta before it: the credit goes back one hop per step under ManualRun.step(dt) (it took two), and a round trip takes about half as long in a free run. The fixed point and the cost of an update are the same; the trajectories differ.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • mujou.testing: use mujou.run_manually instead of mujou.testing.run, and mujou.ManualRun.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • The docstring of pc.TimeConstants.period: one update of the period moves delta to -g with lam = r**2 / (h + r), not h * r / (h + r) (the two agree only for r = h, the default).
The first release. The API works but will still change in breaking ways in the 0.x releases.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Nodes, written in PyTorch: mujou.Node with the lifecycle hooks on_start, on_update(dt), on_pause, on_resume, on_exception and on_stop, and a per-node period (Node(period=...)).
  • Messages between nodes: Port and MultiPort, connected by Channel, with the message specs TensorSpec, DictSpec, IntSpec, FloatSpec, BoolSpec and TimestampSpec. A node reads the latest value its neighbour sent and never waits for it.
  • Networks: Network to connect nodes and Group to put them side by side.
  • Runs: mujou.run(root) runs a network in the background on a pool of worker threads, written in Rust. The handle Run writes inputs, reads outputs, waits for a condition and subscribes to a port from the host program.
  • Time: one timer per run (mujou.time), which can be paused, and a virtual timer for tests.
  • State: Stateful, and state_dict / load_state_dict of a run to save it and resume it later.
  • Errors: an exception in any hook stops the whole run and is raised in the host program as NetworkError.
  • Testing: mujou.testing.run and ManualRun.step to step nodes by hand, deterministically.
  • PC-ALM (Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding): the nodes of mujou.pc (Input, Layer, Output, Chain) and its submodules: the losses loss.MSELoss and loss.CrossEntropyLoss, the weight optimizers optim.SGD and optim.AdamW that advance with time, the relaxation relax.Euler, and the messages msg and the learning clock clock. A layer holds its deviation r as state, and a Chain has a period.
  • CUDA: a node computes on its own device (Node(device=...)). A message between CUDA nodes, and a value that the host writes to a CUDA node, stay on the device when the reader is on CUDA; other messages pass through host memory.
  • Examples: programs from examples/quickstart.py to MNIST and to CIFAR-10 with a ResNet-20 of PC-ALM nodes on a GPU.
  • Visualization: mujou.viz.to_html draws a network as a self-contained HTML page.
  • Wheels for Python 3.14 and the free-threaded 3.14t on Linux (x86_64, aarch64), macOS (arm64) and Windows (x86_64).

docs.text: This page assumes you have used PyTorch's nn.Module and tensors. To start with code, go to Run a Network.

docs.title: From PyTorch
docs.text: PyTorch Mujou You call the model's forward in your loop Mujou calls the node's on_update(dt); you write no loop The arguments and return value of forward A port's recv() and send() You assign submodules to a parent module You assign nodes to a Network model.train() and model.eval() None: inference and learning happen at the same time loss.backward() reaches the whole model Gradients stay inside a node; messages pass between nodes model.state_dict() Each node's state_dict(), and run.state_dict() for the whole run

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> on_start
    on_start --> load_state_dict : on a restore
    on_start --> on_update : on a fresh start
    load_state_dict --> on_update
    on_update --> on_update : every period on average
    on_update --> on_pause : run.state_dict()
    on_pause --> on_resume : after the state is copied
    on_resume --> on_update
    on_update --> on_stop : normal end
    on_update --> on_exception : a hook of any node raised
    on_exception --> on_stop
    on_stop --> [*]

Call super() first in what you override

In __init__ and in every hook, call super().__init__(...) or super().on_update(dt) first (Node).

Inside a node Between nodes Execution Synchronous: ordinary PyTorch code Asynchronous: no node waits for another Exchange Variables and the computation graph Messages through ports (copies, detached from the graph) Gradients Recorded, as plain PyTorch does Never cross

The node class, not a setting, decides how much computation one node holds (one layer, several layers, or a whole model); put layers that should learn together by backpropagation in one node class.

flowchart LR
    subgraph N1["Node 1 (two layers learning together by BP; synchronous inside)"]
        direction LR
        L1["Linear"] --> R["ReLU"] --> L2["Linear"]
    end
    subgraph N2["Node 2"]
        L3["Linear"]
    end
    N1 -. "message (asynchronous)" .-> N2
Why does a node hold no loop?

Mujou runs many nodes on a few worker threads. When a node holds only one update, Mujou decides when and on which thread to call it. That is also what lets it stop every node to take the state, and lets a test update the nodes one step at a time.

docs.title: Ports and channels
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Node A (sends)
    participant C as Channel
    participant B as Node B (reads)
    B->>C: recv()
    C-->>B: the initial value (zeros by default, time None)
    A->>C: send(1)
    A->>C: send(2)
    B->>C: recv()
    C-->>B: 2 (1 was replaced before anyone read it)
    B->>C: recv()
    C-->>B: 2 (the same value again)
    A->>C: send(3)
Why not a queue?

In a queue, values pile up when the sender and the reader run at different rates, and the nodes end up in step with the slower one. When nodes only read and write the latest value, each runs at its own rate without waiting for the others.

A reader never waits: before the peer has sent anything, it gets the initial value, with the time None (Port.recv, Port.recv_with_time).

A port's spec sets the type of its messages, and a value sent arrives as a copy detached from the computation graph.

Use a Port to receive from one peer (it may send to any number), and a MultiPort to gather peers of one role (Kinds of port).

docs.title: Networks and paths
docs.text:
A Network is a container: you assign nodes to its attributes and connect their ports. It runs nothing itself. Assign a child's port to the network's own attribute (prev and next by convention), and the network connects from outside like a node (code in Network).

flowchart TB
    subgraph net["mujou.run(Classifier())"]
        R["Classifier (root)"] -->|body| B["Stack"]
        R -->|head| H["Head<br/>path head"]
        B -->|l1| L1["Hidden<br/>path body.l1"]
        B -->|l2| L2["Hidden<br/>path body.l2"]
    end
    subgraph one["mujou.run(Head())"]
        N["Head (root node)<br/>path #quot;#quot;"]
    end

Paths are the keys of the state tree (for renaming an attribute, see When you resume).

To put several networks side by side in one run, use a Group (Groups).

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
each vertical line = a call to on_update; the interval since the last one is dt the run's timer → Node A dt dt Node B a busy machine only makes dt longer

A run has one time axis, its timer, used by every node and by the host (Time).

The intervals between updates differ between nodes and vary, so on_update moves the state in proportion to the dt it is given, not to the number of calls (Updating in proportion to dt).

docs.title: Learning
docs.text:
Mujou builds no update rule into nodes, ports or the scheduler.

Update rule Where gradients are taken Read Backpropagation in a node Inside one node, with an ordinary loss.backward() Learn in a Node PC-ALM (mujou.pc) Inside each node; neighbors exchange messages Learn with PC-ALM A rule of your own As the node decides Update Rules

docs.title: Rules a node keeps
docs.text:
Rule If you break it Instead Do not block with time.sleep The other nodes' dt grows To update at intervals, period. To wait with no choice, dedicated_thread=True. For the host to wait, run.timer.sleep A node runs once RuntimeError Build new instances to run again (mujou.run) Do not read a node's attributes from the host while it runs It races with the node's updates Read ports with run.read and the state with run.state_dict(). Attributes are readable after the run ends Send nothing that depends on the state in on_start It sends the state from before the restore Send it in the first on_update (load_state_dict comes after on_start; see the diagram in Nodes) Do not change the state in on_stop The state taken after a normal end changes In on_stop, only release resources such as I/O Register plain values and containers of tensors that change while running A restore starts them again Counters, the time last seen, and lists or dicts of tensors go to register_state Keep the computation graph inside one update The graph keeps growing detach the values you carry to the next update, and update parameters inside torch.no_grad() (code below) Do not measure time with self.timer in on_exception and on_stop The run's time stops at the end, so no time passes Measure real time (Node.timer) Only the host moves the time; a node talks only through ports RuntimeError Move the time with the host's run.timer. A node calls neither the methods of Run nor mujou.run, and talks through its own ports 
self.last_y = self.model(x).detach()  # detach values carried to the next update
with torch.no_grad():  # do not record the parameter update
    for p in self.model.parameters():
        p -= lr * p.grad

docs.title: mujou.Network
docs.text:
Bases: Component

A composite of nodes and other networks, declared as attributes.

Assign nodes and networks as attributes and connect their ports with Port.connect. The children of a network are the nodes and networks among its attributes, in the order of assignment: mujou.run reads them when it starts, as nn.Module finds its submodules, so nodes in a list, a tuple or a dict are not children (the run raises TypeError for them). A port assigned to a network is only a reference to it: expose the ports the host uses that way (by convention prev and next, e.g. self.prev = self.l1.prev). A network is only the structure of a run: its nodes still run independently and asynchronously.

mujou.run(net) runs the network; the Run it returns is how the host talks to the running nodes. A node of the network is at the path of its attributes from the root ("body.l1"), which names it in the state tree and in errors.

Example::

class Stack(Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.l1 = Hidden(784, 256)
        self.l2 = Hidden(256, 256)
        self.l1.next.connect(self.l2.prev)
        self.prev = self.l1.prev  # expose the previous side
        self.next = self.l2.next  # expose the next side


class Classifier(Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.body = Stack()
        self.head = Head()  # a node with prev, next and teacher ports
        self.body.next.connect(self.head.prev)  # l2.next <-> head.prev
        self.prev = self.body.prev  # the input
        self.teacher = self.head.teacher  # the target, a port of head


net = Classifier()
with mujou.run(net, inputs={net.prev: x0, net.teacher: y0}) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x, net.teacher: y})  # switch together
    run.timer.sleep(0.1)  # present the input for 0.1 s of the run's time
    prediction = run.read(net.head.next)
    state = run.state_dict()

docs.title: mujou.Group
docs.text:
Group(**children: Node | Network)

Bases: Network

A network of the given nodes and networks side by side, each at its keyword, unconnected unless they were connected before.

The node l1 of Group(enc=a) is at "enc.l1".

Example::

enc, dec = Encoder(), Decoder()
enc.next.connect(dec.prev)
with mujou.run(Group(enc=enc, dec=dec)) as run:
    state = run.state_dict()  # nodes "enc.l1", ..., "dec.l1", ...

docs.title: mujou.Node
docs.text:
Node(
    *,
    period: float = 0.01,
    seed: int | None = None,
    device: Device = "cpu",
    dedicated_thread: bool = False,
)

Bases: Component

A unit of asynchronous computation: the leaf of a network.

Call super().__init__(...) first in __init__ (mujou.run raises TypeError for a node that did not), then declare the node's ports and state as attributes of the instance. A run reads the attributes when it starts. A Port, a MultiPort, a Node or a Network declared as an attribute of the class instead raises TypeError when the class is defined. A node must not hold other nodes or networks as attributes, nor ports in a list, a tuple or a dict (the run raises TypeError); put nodes side by side in a Network instead.

Override the lifecycle hooks below; each does nothing by default. As in any subclass, call the same hook of super() first in each override. The framework calls the hooks on the thread that runs the node (see "Threads" below), in this order:

  • on_start(): once, when the run starts (also when it is restored). Open the node's I/O here. A node with dedicated_thread=True gets it on its own thread, so it can also make its per-thread settings here. Do not send anything that depends on the state here: a restore loads the state after it.
  • load_state_dict(state): only when the run was restored, after on_start and before the first on_update.
  • on_update(dt): repeatedly, once every period on average (see below). dt is the time in seconds on the run's timer since the node's last update. Read the ports with recv, update in proportion to dt, and write the ports with send. It never waits for other nodes.
  • on_pause(): when the node has stopped for the run to take its state (Run.state_dict). on_resume(): when that pause ends, before the next on_update. A pause of the timer (Timer.pause) calls neither: the node only sees no time pass.
  • on_exception(): once on every node, when a hook of any node has raised, before on_stop.
  • on_stop(): once, when the run stops, also after an exception. It must not change what state_dict returns: the state taken after a normal end is the state at the stop.

state_dict() is called when the run's state is taken, while the node is paused (or, after a normal end, on the host's thread that called Run.state_dict). Its ports refuse to receive or send there, so that taking the state is not seen by the other nodes. The framework copies what it returns before the node resumes.

The state of a node is, as for an nn.Module, every attribute that holds a torch.Tensor (nn.Parameter included) or a Stateful (an nn.Module, a pc.clock.LearnClock; not a class), every attribute registered with register_state, and the state of generator. What an attribute holds when the state is taken or loaded decides. The settings that __init__ computes from its arguments (a time constant, say) are no state: a node restored with other arguments keeps its own. Register the plain values that change while the node runs (a counter, the time last seen), and the containers of tensors (a list as a replay buffer, a dict of tensors): a list or a dict is no state by itself, even of tensors. Make the state in __init__ and update it in place: load_state_dict copies into the tensors that the node holds. To choose the state yourself, override both state_dict and load_state_dict: extend what super().state_dict() returns, and pass super().load_state_dict the state without the keys you added.

If any hook raises, the whole run stops. A hook must not call mujou.run or the methods of any Run (write, read, state_dict, ...): they raise RuntimeError there, because a node talks only through its own ports.

Threads: by default the node runs on the workers, a pool of threads that the run shares among its nodes (mujou.run(..., workers=...)). Each hook may then run on a different thread from the previous one, but the hooks of a node never run at the same time, and each sees what the previous one wrote. Whether the next hook sees what a hook set per thread (threading.local, threading.current_thread(), settings of torch such as torch.set_grad_enabled or torch.autocast) depends on the schedule, and the next node on the same worker may see it too: set such settings back before the hook returns (inside a with, say). contextvars do persist: each node runs its hooks in a contextvars.Context of its own, which starts empty (it does not inherit the host's). A hook that blocks (time.sleep, waiting for I/O or a lock) holds its worker meanwhile, and the other nodes' dt grows; give such a node dedicated_thread=True, so that it runs on a thread of its own, with every hook on that thread.

The framework leaves gradient recording as it is, on by default as in plain PyTorch: a hook may call backward directly, and computes without a graph inside with torch.no_grad():. No graph crosses nodes: a port sends a detached copy. Before each hook, when device is CUDA, the framework makes the device and a stream of the node's own current: the only per-thread settings it makes, and around state_dict (which may run on the host's thread) it sets the thread's own back. On CUDA it also waits for the work queued on that stream after on_update (holding its worker meanwhile), after load_state_dict and around state_dict. It does this around the hooks, so overriding one never skips it.

The node updates once every period (0.01 s by default) of the run's timer on average: the time an update takes counts toward the period, and a node that falls a whole period behind does not update several times in a row to catch up. A pause does not count. dt is still the time that actually passed since the last update, longer than period when the node is late, so keep updating in proportion to it and stay stable for the longest dt it can get. A manual run (ManualRun.step) ignores the period.

period=0.0 updates as soon as any time has passed since the last update. Set it only when the node must: such a node keeps a CPU core busy, and takes time from the other nodes, whose dt it makes irregular. period=math.inf never updates by itself: only ManualRun.step updates such a node.

Example::

class Hidden(Node):
    def __init__(self, n_in: int, n_out: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(seed=0)
        x, h = TensorSpec((32, n_in)), TensorSpec((32, n_out))
        # Send W^T eps back and receive x from the previous side (one peer).
        self.prev = Port(send=x, recv=x)
        # Send h forward and receive W^T eps from each next peer (many).
        self.next = MultiPort(send=h, recv=h)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # torch.Tensor
        feedback = self.next.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor]
        ...
        self.next.send(h)
        self.prev.send(wt_eps)


l1, l2 = Hidden(784, 256), Hidden(256, 256)
l1.next.connect(l2.prev)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION period

The time between two updates on average, in seconds of the run's timer. 0.0 updates as soon as any time has passed.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 0.01

seed

The seed of generator. None seeds it nondeterministically.

TYPE: int | None DEFAULT: None

device

Where the node computes: the CPU or a CUDA device (no other device type is supported). Received messages arrive on it. "cuda" without an index is fixed to the host's current CUDA device.

TYPE: Device DEFAULT: 'cpu'

dedicated_thread

Run the node on a thread of its own instead of the run's workers: for a node whose hooks block, or that relies on per-thread state set once (in on_start).

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

device is neither the CPU nor a CUDA device, or is CUDA while CUDA is not available, or period is negative or NaN.

Allocate with it (torch.zeros(..., device=self.device)): the current device in the hooks is this one, but an explicit device states the intent.

docs.title: generator property
docs.text:
generator: Generator

The node's own random generator on device, seeded with seed.

seed sets nothing else: use this generator instead of the global one, which all nodes share (do not call torch.manual_seed in a node), also to initialize modules (nn.init.normal_(w, generator=self.generator)). super().__init__ creates it, so it can be used in __init__ already, and the hooks go on with the same sequence. Its state is part of the node's state, so a restored node goes on with the same sequence too.

docs.title: timer property
docs.text:
timer: ReadOnlyTimer

The reading side of the timer of the run whose hook runs, which measures the dt of its nodes.

Read the time with self.timer.now() in the hooks (state_dict included). The timer is the one given to mujou.run(..., timer=...), the global timer by default, or, for a run restored from a state, a new timer that started at the time of the state (Run.timer). A ReadOnlyTimer only reads: a node does not change the time of its run (Timer.sleep, set_time_scale and VirtualTimer.advance raise RuntimeError in a hook). It stops at the time the run ends, so the hooks that run after the end (on_exception, on_stop) see the time stand still; measure real time there instead. The host reads Run.timer.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

This is not read in a hook of this node while it runs (but in __init__, by the host, or by another node).

docs.title: register_state
docs.text:
register_state(name: str) -> None

Add the attribute name to the state, whatever value it holds.

Use it for the plain values that change while the node runs (a counter, the time last seen) and for the containers of tensors (a list as a replay buffer), which are not state by themselves. The attribute is state while it is assigned, whatever it holds. The default state_dict returns the value as it is, and the default load_state_dict assigns a deep copy of the saved value (or copies into a tensor, or loads into a Stateful, that the attribute holds then).

Register in __init__: a restore loads into new instances, which must have the same state.

The state is data: when the run takes it, it detaches every tensor of what state_dict returns (in its dicts, lists and tuples) and copies the result, so no graph goes with it.

torch.load(..., weights_only=True) reads only basic types (int, float, bool, str, None, and lists, tuples and dicts of them and of tensors): keep the registered values to those if the state is saved with torch.save.

RAISES DESCRIPTION AttributeError

The node has no attribute name (not assigned yet, misspelled, or a property); assign it first.

docs.title: on_start
docs.text:
on_start() -> None

Called once when the run starts (also when it is restored), before any other hook. Do not send anything that depends on the state here: a restore loads it later.

docs.title: on_update
docs.text:
on_update(dt: float) -> None

Called repeatedly with dt, the seconds on the run's timer since the node's last update (always > 0). Read the ports, update in proportion to dt and send.

The first dt counts from when every node's on_start has returned (the start of the run), or, for a restored run, from the node's last update in the state.

docs.title: on_pause
docs.text:
on_pause() -> None

Called when the node has stopped for the run to take its state (Run.state_dict), at the end of its current on_update. A pause of the timer (Timer.pause) does not call it.

docs.title: on_resume
docs.text:
on_resume() -> None

Called when the pause for taking the state ends, before the next on_update.

docs.title: on_exception
docs.text:
on_exception() -> None

Called once on every node when a hook of any node has raised, before on_stop. What it raises is logged and ignored.

docs.title: on_stop
docs.text:
on_stop() -> None

Called once when the run stops, also after an exception. It must not change what state_dict returns. What it raises is logged and ignored.

docs.title: state_dict
docs.text:
state_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

Return the node's state: "generator", the state of generator, then each attribute of the state in the order of assignment, under its name: a tensor detach-ed, the state_dict() of a Stateful, or a registered value as it is.

The tensors share memory with the attributes (the framework copies the tree). requires_grad and .grad are not part of the state, as in nn.Module.state_dict.

docs.title: load_state_dict
docs.text:
load_state_dict(state: Mapping[str, Any]) -> None

Restore state, as the default state_dict returned it, into the attributes of the state, without recording gradients: copy_ into each tensor, load_state_dict into each Stateful, and assign a copy.deepcopy of the saved value to any other registered attribute, with the tensors in it (in its dicts, lists and tuples) moved to device.

The objects stay the same, so references taken in __init__ or on_start see the restored values, and a tensor that records gradients stays a leaf that does. copy_ casts the dtype and moves the device. The state of generator is set as it is saved, and a generator keeps its state in a format of its device's type: the state must come from a node on the same type of device (the CPU or CUDA).

An override that keeps a tensor of state as it is shares its memory with the tree given to mujou.run(..., state=...): copy it instead.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

The keys of state are not those of this node's state, or a tensor's shape differs.

docs.title: mujou.Stateful
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

An object with a state of its own, which a node keeps in its state.

An attribute of a Node that holds a Stateful is in the node's state by itself: the default Node.state_dict returns its state_dict() under the attribute's name, and Node.load_state_dict passes that back to its load_state_dict. An object is one by inheriting this class, not by having methods of these names. nn.Module is registered as one; register a class of another library with Stateful.register(cls).

Example::

class Counter(mujou.Stateful):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.n = 0

    def state_dict(self) -> dict[str, int]:
        return {"n": self.n}

    def load_state_dict(self, state: Mapping[str, int]) -> None:
        self.n = state["n"]

Return the state. Its tensors may share memory with the object's: the run copies the state it takes.

docs.title: mujou.Port
docs.text:
Port(
    *,
    send: MessageSpec[S] | None = None,
    recv: MessageSpec[R] | None = None,
    initial: S | None = None,
)

Bases: _Port[S, R]

A connection point that sends messages of type S and receives at most one peer's messages of type R.

Declare ports as attributes of a node in __init__. send is the spec of what the port sends and recv the spec of what it receives; omit one for a one-way port (its message type is then Never). recv() returns one message, so a port that receives takes one peer; a port that only sends takes any number, and send reaches them all. To receive from several peers of one kind, use a MultiPort; for inputs of different roles, use one port each.

Two ports connect when the send of each equals the recv of the other. A port may stay unconnected: the host then writes what it receives (Run.write).

initial is what the port has sent before its first send: what its peers receive and the host reads until then. A run copies it when it starts. Without it, that is zeros. A restored run takes the values from the state instead.

A run names the port in its errors by the path of its node and its attribute ("body.l1.next"; "Shift.next" for a port of the node run as the root).

Example::

class Sensor(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.next = Port(send=TensorSpec((3,)), initial=torch.ones(3))


class Monitor(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = Port(recv=TensorSpec((3,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # torch.Tensor; ones until the sensor sends


sensor, monitor = Sensor(), Monitor()
sensor.next.connect(monitor.prev)

docs.title: connect
docs.text:
connect(other: Port[R, S] | MultiPort[R, S]) -> Channel

Connect this port to other and return the channel between them.

The channel is registered at both ports, so each sends to and receives from the other. Connecting the same two ports again, in either order, returns the same channel. A port may connect to itself.

RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

The specs are not mutually reversed: self.send_spec != other.recv_spec or self.recv_spec != other.send_spec.

ValueError

A Port that receives would get a second peer (use a MultiPort to receive from several).

docs.title: send
docs.text:
send(msg: S) -> None

Send msg to every peer and to what the host reads (Run.read).

msg must match the send spec exactly; tensor dtypes are never converted (a scalar is taken as Python's typing takes it: an int for a float). The values are detached and copied, so changing msg afterwards changes nothing that was sent. If a node on CUDA reads the port, a tensor on the node's CUDA device is copied on the device, on the node's stream, and send waits for that stream before the peers can read it; a peer on CUDA copies it from device to device. It stays on the device also while the hook has made another device current (torch.cuda.device(...)). Any other CUDA tensor is copied to the host. It never waits for the peers to read.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

The caller is not a hook of the node that owns the port, while it runs (or is its state_dict).

TypeError

A value is not of its field's kind (a torch.Tensor for a TensorSpec, an int for an IntSpec, ...), or a DictSpec message is not a dict with the spec's keys.

ValueError

A shape or a dtype differs from the spec.

OverflowError

An int is out of the range of its IntSpec.

BufferError

A tensor is not dense (torch.strided).

docs.title: recv
docs.text:
recv() -> R

Return the latest message received, without waiting for a new one.

The message comes from the peer's send; an unconnected port reads what the host writes with Run.write instead. Until that writer first writes, it is the initial value: the peer port's initial, or else zeros. For a port the host writes, it is the value in inputs of mujou.run, or else zeros. A restored run takes it from state. recv_with_time tells whether the writer has written yet.

Every call copies into new tensors on the owning node's device, without gradients, so changing them in place changes nothing else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

The caller is not a hook of the node that owns the port, while it runs (or is its state_dict).

docs.title: recv_with_time
docs.text:
recv_with_time() -> tuple[R, _native.Timestamp | None]

Like recv, but return (message, time).

time is the Timestamp on the run's timer at which the writer wrote the message, or None while the writer has not written yet (the message is then the initial value). The writer is the peer (its send or send_to), or the host for an unconnected port (inputs of mujou.run or Run.write). A restored run keeps the times of the state, None included. Raises as recv does.

docs.title: mujou.MultiPort
docs.text:
MultiPort(
    *,
    send: MessageSpec[S] | None = None,
    recv: MessageSpec[R] | None = None,
    initial: S | None = None,
)

Bases: _Port[S, R]

A connection point that sends messages of type S and receives messages of type R from any number of peers of one kind.

It is declared and connected as a Port is, but recv() returns {channel: message}, one entry per peer in connection order, and send_to sends to one peer. Use it to merge or to branch peers that play the same role; for inputs of different roles (a prediction and an error, say), use one Port each. The host does not write to a MultiPort.

Example::

class Sum(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = MultiPort(recv=TensorSpec((3,)))
        self.next = Port(send=TensorSpec((3,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(sum(self.prev.recv().values(), torch.zeros(3)))

docs.text:

One connection between two ports, which connect makes.

docs.title: mujou.MessageSpec
docs.text:
Bases: Generic[_M]

The spec of a message of type _M.

TensorSpec is a MessageSpec[torch.Tensor], IntSpec a MessageSpec[int] and DictSpec(Sample, ...) a MessageSpec[Sample]. Annotate with it a function that takes any spec::

def sender[T](spec: MessageSpec[T]) -> Port[T]:
    return Port(send=spec)

docs.title: mujou.TensorSpec
docs.text:
TensorSpec(shape: Sequence[int], dtype: dtype = torch.float32)

Bases: MessageSpec[Tensor]

The shape and the dtype of a message that is one torch.Tensor.

Every dimension is at least 1, and () is a scalar. A batch dimension is just a part of the shape. The dtype is torch.float32 unless given, whatever torch.get_default_dtype() is.

Two specs are equal when their shapes and dtypes are equal. A message whose shape or dtype differs from the spec is an error; dtypes are never converted. A spec has no device: a message of the spec may be on any device.

zeros, rand and empty make a tensor of the spec, on the CPU unless device says otherwise. For any other initial value, fill one of them in place (spec.empty().fill_(0.5)).

Example::

spec = TensorSpec((32, 256))  # float32
spec = TensorSpec((32, 256), torch.bfloat16)
x0 = spec.zeros()
noise = TensorSpec((4,)).rand(generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
ones = spec.empty(device="cuda").fill_(1.0)
RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

dtype is not in dtypes.

docs.text:
DictSpec(typed_dict: type[TD], /, **specs: FieldSpec)

Bases: MessageSpec[TD]

The spec of a message that is a TypedDict of fields.

Give the TypedDict class and one FieldSpec per key: a TensorSpec for a key annotated as torch.Tensor, IntSpec for int, FloatSpec for float, BoolSpec for bool and TimestampSpec for Timestamp. Every key of the TypedDict is required (no nesting), and the keyword arguments name exactly its keys. The keys keep the order in which the TypedDict defines them.

Two specs are equal when they use the same TypedDict class and equal specs for every key.

Example::

class Feedback(TypedDict):
    error: torch.Tensor
    count: int

msg: Feedback = spec.zeros()
error = spec.field("error", TensorSpec)  # a TensorSpec, to type checkers too
RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

docs.title: mujou.pc
docs.text:
PC-ALM (augmented Lagrangian predictive coding) as nodes of mujou.

Each node holds a part of the model and learns from its neighbors' messages only: Input takes the samples the host writes, each Layer wraps a module as one constraint h = f(h_in), and Output holds the last module and the loss. Inside a node, the module is differentiated by autograd; between nodes, activities (Activity, the predictions of the forward pass) flow to the next node and gradients of the energy to the previous one. The target of each sample travels with its input in the Activity, so the output node pairs every prediction with its own target. Chain connects the nodes for a sequence of modules, and show shows it a sample. Each node gives the spec of what it sends as act_spec, which the next node takes, to build other shapes by hand.

The names that go with a role are in a submodule, which this package imports:

  • pc.optim: SGD and AdamW set how the parameters of a node move in time (Optimizer); each node binds the setting to its own parameters (BoundOptimizer).
  • pc.relax: Euler sets how the deviation r = h - mu of a node moves (Relaxer); each node binds the setting to its own r (BoundRelaxer).
  • pc.loss: MSELoss and CrossEntropyLoss give the loss of each sample.
  • pc.msg: Sample, Activity, Prediction and activity_spec, what the nodes send.
  • pc.clock: LearnClock and Tick.
  • pc.functional: the parts the nodes are made of, for writing nodes of your own.

The samples are independent and the shapes start with the batch, batch: () (the default) for one sample at a time, B for B samples, or a shape of several dimensions.

Import it as a submodule::

import mujou.pc as pc

B = 64
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU()),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.loss.CrossEntropyLoss(B),
    tau=pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3),
    optimizer=pc.optim.SGD(tau=1.28),
    learn_interval=0.15,
)

Bases: Network, Shown

Input -> Layer -> ... -> Output: a network that learns modules in sequence by PC-ALM, as nn.Sequential(*modules) would compute them.

modules[:-1] each become a Layer and modules[-1] the Output, after an Input of the samples x and targets y. Each node takes the act_spec of the one before and the nodes are connected in order. The children are input, layer0, ..., output (modules[i] is in layer{i}, also layers[i]), which are also their paths in Run.state_dict(). Every node runs with the same period, tau.period (tau.h / 2 with tau.r = tau.h) unless given; for a period of its own for each node, build the nodes one by one (show shows them samples too).

The host writes a Sample to prev and reads a Prediction from next, or does both with show.

Example::

B = 64
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU()),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.loss.CrossEntropyLoss(B),
    tau=pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3),
    optimizer=pc.optim.SGD(tau=1.28),
    learn_interval=0.15,
)
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    prediction = pc.show(run, net, sample, seconds=0.2)

Bases: Node

A node that takes the samples the host writes and sends them on as the Activity of the next node, with their targets.

The host writes a Sample (x, y and mask) to prev with Run.write. In each on_update the node sends from next an Activity whose h is x, with y, mask and the time (ns) at which the host wrote them: the nodes on the path pass them on with the activity computed from x, so that the output node pairs each prediction with its own target. A new time tells them the input changed. x is clamped: what the next node sends back on next is not read.

Before the host first writes, the node sends zeros with mask False and time 0. It holds no state of its own: what it sends is the last write. act_spec is the spec of what the node sends, for the next node.

Example::

B = 64
inp = pc.Input(
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    period=1e-3,
    batch=B,
)
...
mask = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({inp.prev: {"x": x, "y": y, "mask": mask}})

docs.title: Layer
docs.text:
Layer(
    module: Module,
    *,
    act_spec: DictSpec[Activity],
    tau: TimeConstants,
    optimizer: Optimizer,
    relaxer: Relaxer = Euler(),
    learn_interval: float | None,

    device: Device = "cpu",
    cuda_graph: bool = False,

Bases: Node

A node that wraps module as one constraint h = f(h_in; theta) of PC-ALM.

It predicts mu = module(h_in) from the activity h_in of the previous node and sends it on: the activity of every node is the forward pass. It holds the deviation \(r = h - \mu\) of its activity and the dual lam of the constraint, which stay in the node and make the credit it sends back. With \(\delta = r + \lambda\) and the sum \(g\) of what the next nodes send back:

\[ \tau_h \dot r = -(r + \lambda + g) - \frac{\tau_h}{\tau_r}\,r,\qquad \tau_\lambda \dot\lambda = r, \]

and theta moves by optimizer (such as pc.optim.SGD, \(\tau_\theta \dot\theta = -g_\theta / B\)) with the mean gradient \(g_\theta / B\), where \(B\) is the number of samples in the batch (1 without one), \(g_\theta = -J_\theta^\top \delta\) and the node sends \(g_{\mathrm{in}} = -J_h^\top \delta\) to the previous node (both from one vector-Jacobian product of module, functional.vjp). At a fixed point, \(r = 0\) and lam is the credit \(-\partial\ell/\partial h\) of backpropagation. Inside the node, module is differentiated by autograd; between nodes, only these messages flow.

Sending mu rather than mu + r is the fixed prediction assumption of predictive coding: it keeps the fixed point, and the credit flows down the path only. Were r sent up, it would move the activities of the nodes above and come back as credit through the product of their Jacobians, a loop that diverges in chains whose forward pass amplifies, however short the steps. With the defaults of TimeConstants (period = tau.h / 2, tau.lam = tau.h / 2, tau.r = tau.h), delta follows -g in one update, which is also when it is passed on to the previous node: the credit takes at most one period per hop.

Whatever moves mu (a new sample, an update of theta here or below), r and lam stay and only relax, unless the sample starts anew: in the update that first sees an input, the node sets r and lam of the samples whose reset is set to zero (Sample). The same update still relaxes them with the g of the next nodes, which have not yet seen the input, so it passes the credit of the sample before down once more (delta = -g with the defaults); that credit is gone within the round trip, before the node learns. Without a target, r and lam decay to 0.

Each on_update(dt):

  1. reads the activity and ticks its clock, which caps dt at max_dt; with a new input, sets r and lam of the samples it resets to zero;
  2. moves r and then lam by dt with the g the next nodes sent (functional.relax_);
  3. computes mu, g_in and, when it learns, g_theta with the delta it has just relaxed, zero for the samples whose mask is False, and sends g_in;
  4. sends h = mu, and the y, mask, reset and time that came with h_in;
  5. when it learns, moves theta by the time since its last update (optimizer.step_).

Its clock (a LearnClock) tells when it learns: in its first update once learn_interval seconds have passed since the host wrote the input (its time, on the run's time), and then every learn_interval seconds while the input stays, but never in the update that first sees an input (the g it relaxes with is still that of the input before); with learn_interval=None, in every update; with math.inf, never. The nodes read the one timer of the run, so the nodes on a path learn at about the same time, however deep they are, and each from the relaxed delta of the same input. The input goes forward, and the credit back, at most one period per hop (exactly one step per hop under ManualRun.step(dt)). A learn_interval longer than the round trip (2 * hops * period, with hops the number of connections from the Input to the Output) is recommended, so that the nodes learn from the relaxed delta. A free run of equal periods without jitter often goes round in about hops * period, but only the bound holds in general. The node does not learn when no sample of the input has a target (every mask is False): that time is dropped from the next update, which would otherwise learn from the delta left over from an earlier input. Nor does it keep the time of an input that changed before the node learned from it. Until the first sample reaches the node, the activity is zeros (mask all False, time 0), so it does not learn then.

dt is capped because the step is explicit: after a long stall (a loaded machine), a long dt / tau.h would overshoot and make r and lam diverge. The time beyond max_dt is dropped, from the relaxation and from the weight of the next update of theta alike. The default tau.max_dt is the step that settles delta (tau.h / 2 with tau.r = tau.h).

With cuda_graph, the node records the vector-Jacobian product of module in a torch.cuda.CUDAGraph (one without and one with the gradients of the parameters, each at the first update that needs it) and replays it in every update: it copies h_in and delta into the graph's buffers and reads mu, g_in and g_theta from them. The update is the same as without it, bit for bit, with far fewer kernels launched from the CPU, which bound an update on a GPU with a small batch. module must then run the same kernels on every input of the spec: no synchronization with the host (.item(), a branch on a tensor's value) and parameters updated in place, as pc.optim does. The graphs are not part of the state: a node made again from a state dict records them anew.

relaxer sets how r moves along the force on it (functional.relax_): the plain step of pc.relax.Euler, or a relaxer of your own with the same fixed point. The node calls the reset_ of the bound relaxer with each new input, with the samples it resets (whose state the relaxer forgets).

module must treat the samples of the batch independently (no BatchNorm in training mode): the gradient of each sample must be its own. It must also be deterministic (no Dropout): mu is what the node sends. Its parameters that require gradients learn; set requires_grad to False to freeze one. It is called once on zeros when the node is made, to find the shape and dtype of h.

The state (Run.state_dict()["nodes"][path]["state"]) holds "generator" (the state of the node's generator), "module" (its state_dict), "r" and "lam" ((*batch, *out)), when to learn ("clock", the state of the LearnClock), the state of optimizer ("optimizer", such as the moments of pc.optim.AdamW) and that of relaxer ("relaxer", empty for pc.relax.Euler). The h it sent last is in the state of its port next. To watch the node while it runs, read them there: Run.state_dict() pauses the run, whereas reading module, r or lam from the host's thread races with the node's updates in place. act_spec is the spec of what the node sends, for the next node.

Example::

B = 64
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3)
inp = pc.Input(
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    period=tau.period,
    batch=B,
)
hidden = pc.Layer(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU()),
    act_spec=inp.act_spec,
    tau=tau,
    optimizer=pc.optim.SGD(tau=1.28),
    learn_interval=24e-3,
)
inp.next.connect(hidden.prev)
hidden.next.connect(out.prev)  # out: a pc.Output, or another pc.Layer
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION module

The function f, (*batch, *in) -> (*batch, *out), on device.

TYPE: Module

act_spec

The spec of the activity h_in it receives: the act_spec of the node before, which also gives the batch.

TYPE: DictSpec[Activity]

tau

The time constants of r and lam.

TYPE: TimeConstants

optimizer

How theta moves (pc.optim.SGD, pc.optim.AdamW or an Optimizer of your own). The node binds it to its parameters that require gradients and holds the bound optimizer as optimizer.

TYPE: Optimizer

relaxer

How r moves along the force on it (pc.relax.Euler, the default, or a Relaxer of your own). The node binds it to its r and holds the bound relaxer as relaxer.

TYPE: Relaxer DEFAULT: Euler()

learn_interval

The time in seconds from the write of an input to the update of theta, and between the updates while the input stays; longer than 2 * hops * period is recommended. None updates in every on_update, for a stream whose input changes at every frame (good values for it have not been measured yet); math.inf never updates.

TYPE: float | None

period

The period of the node in seconds; None is tau.period (tau.h / 2 with tau.r = tau.h). It must not be longer than max_dt.

TYPE: float | None DEFAULT: None

max_dt

The longest dt an update counts, in seconds; None is tau.max_dt.

TYPE: float | None DEFAULT: None

device

Where the node computes.

TYPE: Device DEFAULT: 'cpu'

cuda_graph

Replay the vector-Jacobian product of module from a CUDA graph (above); the node must be on CUDA.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

The output of module does not start with the batch of act_spec, or LearnClock raises: learn_interval is neither None nor > 0, max_dt is not > 0, or period is longer than max_dt, or cuda_graph is set for a node that is not on CUDA. module raises as PyTorch does when it does not take the h of act_spec on device.

    module: Module,
    *,

    loss: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor],

Bases: Node

A node that predicts y_hat = module(h_in) and whose energy is the loss of the samples that have a target.

It pairs h_in with the target y and mask of the same Activity, so the prediction always meets the target of the very input it was computed from, however fast the host writes. With

\[ \ell = \sum_b \mathrm{mask}_b\, \ell_b(\hat y_b, y_b), \]

theta moves by optimizer with the mean gradient \(\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta}\) (pc.optim.SGD makes it \(\tau_\theta \dot\theta = -\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta}\)), where \(B\) is the number of samples in the batch (1 without one), and it sends \(g_{\mathrm{in}} = \partial\ell/\partial h_{\mathrm{in}}\) to the previous node (functional.loss_vjp): zero for a sample without a target while its y_hat is finite. Each on_update(dt) caps dt at max_dt as Layer does, reads the Activity, sends g_in, sends a Prediction (y_hat with the y, mask and time it was paired with) for the host to read, and updates theta when it learns.

It learns as Layer does, by its clock: once learn_interval seconds have passed since the host wrote the input, but not in the update that first sees it, or in every update with None. When no sample has a target, it does not learn and drops the time since the last update; so too before the first sample arrives, while the activity is zeros (mask all False), and when the input changes before it has learned from it. B is the number of samples in the batch, not the number of samples with a target: a sample without one adds zero.

loss returns the loss of each sample, of the shape of the batch (that of mask), such as MSELoss(batch) or CrossEntropyLoss(batch), and the node sums them. A loss that averages over the batch (such as nn.MSELoss()) would scale the gradient that flows back by 1 / B, so the node refuses it when it is made: it calls module and loss once on zeros then (functional.loss_vjp), which also finds the shape of y_hat. module must treat the samples independently, as in Layer.

The state holds "generator", "module", when to learn ("clock") and the state of optimizer ("optimizer"). Read it with Run.state_dict(), as for Layer.

Example::

out = pc.Output(
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
    act_spec=hidden.act_spec,  # hidden: a pc.Layer
    loss=pc.loss.CrossEntropyLoss(B),
    tau=tau,
    optimizer=pc.optim.SGD(tau=1.28),
    learn_interval=24e-3,
)
hidden.next.connect(out.prev)
# The host: prediction = run.read(out.next); prediction["y_hat"], ...

max_dt

As in Layer: the longest dt an update counts, here towards the weight of the update of theta. The default tau.max_dt is that of Layer, so that every node of a chain counts the same time.

docs.title: TimeConstants dataclass
docs.text:
TimeConstants(*, h: float, lam: float, r: float)

The time constants of the continuous-time PC-ALM, in seconds.

A node sends its prediction mu and holds the deviation \(r = h - \mu\) of its activity from it and the dual lam, which it relaxes with

\[ \tau_h \dot r = -(r + \lambda + g) - \frac{\tau_h}{\tau_r}\,r,\qquad \tau_\lambda \dot\lambda = r, \]

and a step of dt seconds moves them by dt / tau of the right-hand side (the discrete step sizes are eta_h = dt / h and alpha = dt / lam). The parameters theta move by the optimizer of the node (pc.optim.SGD or pc.optim.AdamW), which holds their time constant.

lam=math.inf makes the dual stay at zero (alpha = 0); with r=math.inf too, the nodes are those of predictive coding with the fixed prediction assumption, whose error r settles at the credit of backpropagation (the decay would shrink it by 1 + h / r at each node). h must be finite.

r is the time constant of the decay of the deviation. The fixed point stays (lam integrates r, so r = 0 there, and lam is the credit of backpropagation). The nodes send mu, so the credit flows down the path only, and the steps are stable in any chain once they are in each node. The defaults are chosen together: with r = h, lam = h / 2 and a period of h / 2, one update moves delta = r + lam to -g exactly, so the credit takes at most one period per hop and does not overshoot (a larger step overshoots, and the overshoot grows at every node). An analog integrator that holds r and leaks is this decay.

The fields are keyword-only and have no defaults: all are floats, and a swap by position could not be caught by the type checker.

Example::

tau = TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3)  # a period of 2e-3
pc_only = TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=math.inf, r=math.inf)
RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

h is not finite and > 0, or lam or r is not > 0 (NaN is not).

docs.text: h: float

docs.title: lam instance-attribute
docs.text: lam: float

docs.title: r instance-attribute

docs.title: period property
docs.text:
period: float

The default period of a node, h / (1 + h / r): the step that moves r all the way along its own pull (h / 2 with r = h, h without the decay). With lam = r**2 / (h + r) (h / 2 with r = h) and max_dt equal to it (2 r >= h), one update of this dt moves delta = r + lam to -g, whatever r and lam were.

docs.title: max_dt property
docs.text:
max_dt: float

The default longest dt an update counts, min(h / (1 + h / r), 2 * lam) (the default period unless the dual is faster): the explicit Euler step of r then lam is then stable (specs/pc.md, "dt の打ち切り"). Every node of a chain caps at the same time, so that they weigh their updates of the parameters alike.

docs.title: show
docs.text:
show(run: Run, chain: Shown, sample: Sample, *, seconds: float) -> Prediction

Return the prediction chain makes for sample before it learns from it (a prequential prediction), after showing it seconds long.

chain is a Shown: a Chain, or a network of the nodes of mujou.pc built by hand that inherits Shown. Writes sample to chain.prev, waits for the first prediction the host reads for that write, and returns it once seconds (of run.timer) have passed since the write, while the nodes learn from the sample (Sample.mask True) or only relax towards it (every mask False, as to evaluate, where a seconds that lets the input reach the output is enough). A node learns from a sample from its second update with it on (learn_interval after the write, when set), and the first prediction of the sample is made of the first activities with it, so the prediction comes before learning unless the host reads it later than that.

Nothing moves the timer of a ManualRun, so there it does not return.

Example::

mask = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)
sample = pc.msg.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=mask, reset=mask)  # shuffled
p = pc.show(run, net, sample, seconds=0.2)
correct = int((p["y_hat"].argmax(1) == y).sum())
RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

A tensor of sample has another shape or dtype than the spec of chain.prev.

TypeError

sample lacks a key, or has one too many.

RuntimeError

The run shut down normally before the prediction.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: mujou.pc.optim
docs.text:
The optimizers that move the parameters of a node in time: SGD (with an optional momentum), RMSProp and AdamW, and TimeScaled, which runs another optimizer on a scaled time.

An optimizer here is a setting (Optimizer): a frozen value that holds no state and may be shared by every node. A node binds it to its own parameters with bind(params), which returns the BoundOptimizer that holds the state (the moments) and moves the parameters by step_(grads, elapsed). The time constants are in seconds, so the flow does not depend on how often the node learns: elapsed is the time the step weighs.

They do not use torch.optim: its optimizers count steps rather than time, in a float32 tensor (with torch's default dtype) that stops growing after 2**24 steps (about 4.7 days when learning every 24 ms); and making one imports torch._dynamo, which brings the GIL back for the whole process in a free-threaded Python (3.14t).

docs.title: Optimizer
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

The setting of how the parameters of a node move in time.

It holds values only, no state, so the nodes may share it. bind(params) makes the BoundOptimizer of the parameters of one node, which holds the state. Give it only the parameters that learn (pc.Layer and pc.Output bind those that require gradients).

An optimizer of your own inherits this class, and its bound optimizer BoundOptimizer, and implements every abstract method of both: a class that misses one raises TypeError when it is instantiated (as any abc.ABC). For example, SGD with a learning rate per step rather than per second::

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StepSGD(pc.optim.Optimizer):
    lr: float

    def bind(self, params):
        return _BoundStepSGD(list(params), self.lr)

class _BoundStepSGD(pc.optim.BoundOptimizer):
    def __init__(self, params, lr):
        self._params, self._lr = params, lr

    def step_(self, grads, elapsed):
        with torch.no_grad():
            for p, g in zip(self._params, grads, strict=True):
                p.sub_(g, alpha=self._lr)

    def state_dict(self):
        return {}

    def load_state_dict(self, state):
        pass

docs.title: BoundOptimizer
docs.text:

An optimizer bound to the parameters of one node, which holds its state.

It holds the parameters by reference. The node that bound it owns it and calls it from its own hooks only. It is a Stateful, so an attribute of a node that holds it is in the node's state by itself: state_dict returns the state with tensors that share memory with the optimizer's, and load_state_dict copies the tensors of the state into those (it keeps none of the state it is given).

docs.title: SGD dataclass
docs.text:
SGD(*, tau: float, tau_m: float | None = None)

Bases: Optimizer

Gradient descent in time, \(\tau_\theta \dot\theta = -g\), with an optional momentum.

A step of elapsed seconds is one step of SGD with the learning rate elapsed / tau: p -= (elapsed / tau) * g. With \(\Delta t\) seconds between two updates of the parameters (the time each input is shown, for a node that learns once from each), the step is of the learning rate Δt / tau. Without tau_m, the bound optimizer has no state (an empty state_dict).

With tau_m, the parameters descend along the gradient averaged over about the last \(\tau_m\) seconds instead:

\[ \tau_m \dot m = g - m,\qquad \tau_\theta \dot\theta = -\hat m, \]

where \(\hat m = m / c_m\) corrects the bias of the moment that starts at zero, with the mass \(\tau_m \dot c_m = 1 - c_m\) from \(c_m = 0\), as in AdamW. A step of elapsed \(= \Delta t\) seconds moves \(m\) and \(c_m\) exactly as the flow would with \(g\) held over \(\Delta t\) (\(m \leftarrow m + a_m (g - m)\) and \(c_m \leftarrow c_m + a_m (1 - c_m)\) with \(a_m = 1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau_m}\)), then \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - (\Delta t / \tau_\theta)\,\hat m\). With a constant \(g\), \(\hat m = g\), and the step is that of SGD without momentum: the momentum averages the gradient and leaves the learning rate as it is. \(\tau_m \to 0\) is SGD without momentum. A step of elapsed == 0 moves nothing.

With a constant \(\Delta t\) and \(\beta = e^{-\Delta t/\tau_m}\), the steps are those of torch.optim.SGD(lr=Δt / tau, momentum=β, dampening=β) (its buffer is then \(m \leftarrow \beta m + (1 - \beta) g\)) up to the bias correction: torch starts its buffer at the first gradient instead of dividing by \(c_m\). The two agree for a constant \(g\), and from the same \(m\) once \(c_m = 1\); otherwise their difference decays as \(\beta^t\) after \(t\) steps.

The state (state_dict()) holds the moment "m" (a list of tensors, of the dtype and device of the parameters) and the mass "c_m" (a Python float in [0, 1]). There is no count of steps.

Example::

hidden = pc.Layer(module, act_spec=..., tau=tau,
                  optimizer=pc.optim.SGD(tau=0.3), learn_interval=24e-3)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION tau

The time constant \(\tau_\theta\) of the parameters, in seconds.

TYPE: float

tau_m

The time constant \(\tau_m\) of the momentum, in seconds, or None for none.

TYPE: float | None DEFAULT: None

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

tau is not finite and > 0, or tau_m is given and is not finite and > 0. Never to learn, give the node learn_interval=math.inf.

docs.title: RMSProp dataclass
docs.text:
RMSProp(*, tau: float, tau_v: float, eps: float = 1e-08)

Bases: Optimizer

RMSProp in time: the gradient divided by the root of a mean square that decays with a time constant.

With the gradient \(g\) (averaged over the batch):

\[ \tau_v \dot v = g^2 - v,\qquad \tau_\theta \dot\theta = -\frac{g}{\sqrt{\hat v} + \varepsilon}, \]

where \(\hat v = v / c_v\) corrects the bias of the moment that starts at zero, with the mass \(\tau_v \dot c_v = 1 - c_v\) from \(c_v = 0\), as in AdamW. A step of elapsed \(= \Delta t\) seconds moves \(v\) and \(c_v\) exactly as the flow would with \(g\) held over \(\Delta t\) (\(v \leftarrow v + a_v (g^2 - v)\) and \(c_v \leftarrow c_v + a_v (1 - c_v)\) with \(a_v = 1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau_v}\)), then \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,g / (\sqrt{\hat v} + \varepsilon)\) with \(\eta = \Delta t / \tau_\theta\). A step of elapsed == 0 moves nothing. There is no momentum and no weight decay.

With a constant \(\Delta t\), the steps are those of torch.optim.RMSprop(lr=Δt / tau, alpha=exp(-Δt / tau_v), eps=eps) up to the bias correction: torch starts its mean square at zero and does not divide it by \(c_v\), so its first steps are larger. The two agree once \(c_v = 1\); their difference decays as \(\alpha^t\) after \(t\) steps.

The state (state_dict()) holds the moment "v" (a list of tensors, of the dtype and device of the parameters) and the mass "c_v" (a Python float in [0, 1]). There is no count of steps.

Like AdamW, a step moves each element by up to about \(\eta\) whatever the size of its gradient.

Example (lr = 1e-3 and alpha = 0.99 of torch, learning once from each input, shown for 32 ms)::

hidden = pc.Layer(module, act_spec=..., tau=tau,
                  optimizer=pc.optim.RMSProp(tau=32e-3 / 1e-3, tau_v=3.2),
                  learn_interval=24e-3)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION tau

The time constant \(\tau_\theta\) of the parameters, in seconds.

TYPE: float

tau_v

The time constant \(\tau_v\) of the mean square, in seconds.

TYPE: float

eps

The \(\varepsilon\) added to \(\sqrt{\hat v}\). It is > 0, so that an element whose gradient has been 0 does not become 0 / 0.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 1e-08

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

tau, tau_v or eps is not finite and > 0.

docs.title: AdamW dataclass
docs.text:
AdamW(
    *,
    tau: float,
    tau_m: float,
    tau_v: float,
    eps: float = 1e-08,
    weight_decay: float = 0.01,
)

Bases: Optimizer

AdamW in time: moments that decay with time constants, and decoupled weight decay.

With the gradient \(g\) (averaged over the batch):

\[ \tau_m \dot m = g - m,\qquad \tau_v \dot v = g^2 - v,\qquad \tau_\theta \dot\theta = -\left(\frac{\hat m}{\sqrt{\hat v} + \varepsilon} + w\,\theta\right), \]

where \(\hat m = m / c_m\) and \(\hat v = v / c_v\) correct the bias of the moments that start at zero, with the masses \(\tau_m \dot c_m = 1 - c_m\) and \(\tau_v \dot c_v = 1 - c_v\) from \(c = 0\): \(c\) is the share of the moment made of gradients so far (the rest is the zero it started from), \(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\) for gradients seen over the time \(t\).

A step of elapsed \(= \Delta t\) seconds moves the moments and masses exactly as the flow would with \(g\) held over \(\Delta t\) (\(m \leftarrow m + a_m (g - m)\) and \(c_m \leftarrow c_m + a_m (1 - c_m)\) with \(a_m = 1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau_m}\), the same for \(v\)), so that two steps of \(\Delta t\) and one of \(2\Delta t\) give the same moments for the same \(g\). \(\theta\) then steps with \(\eta = \Delta t / \tau_\theta\), in the order of torch.optim.AdamW: the decay first, on the \(\theta\) before the step, and the Adam term with the moments and masses just moved:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta (1 - \eta w) - \eta\,\frac{\hat m}{\sqrt{\hat v} + \varepsilon}. \]

A step of elapsed == 0 moves nothing.

With a constant \(\Delta t\), \(1 - a = e^{-\Delta t/\tau}\) is the \(\beta\) of torch.optim.AdamW and \(c = 1 - \beta^t\) its bias correction after \(t\) steps: the steps are those of torch.optim.AdamW(lr=Δt / tau, betas=(exp(-Δt / tau_m), exp(-Δt / tau_v)), eps=eps, weight_decay=weight_decay), up to rounding. From the \(\beta\) of a node that learns every \(\Delta t\), \(\tau_m = -\Delta t / \ln\beta_1\): learning every 32 ms, \(\beta_1 = 0.9\) is about 0.30 s and \(\beta_2 = 0.999\) about 32 s.

weight_decay \(w\) has no unit, and decays \(\theta\) with the time constant \(\tau_\theta / w\), as weight_decay does with lr in torch.optim.AdamW.

The state (state_dict()) holds the moments "m" and "v" (a list of tensors each, of the dtype and device of the parameters) and the masses "c_m" and "c_v" (Python floats in [0, 1]). There is no count of steps.

A step moves each element by about \(\eta\) whatever the size of its gradient, so tau is Δt / lr for the lr of Adam, with \(\Delta t\) the time between two updates of the parameters.

Example (lr = 1e-3, learning once from each input, shown for 32 ms)::

hidden = pc.Layer(module, act_spec=..., tau=tau,
                  optimizer=pc.optim.AdamW(tau=32e-3 / 1e-3, tau_m=0.3,
                                     tau_v=30.0),
                  learn_interval=24e-3)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION tau

The time constant \(\tau_\theta\) of the parameters, in seconds.

TYPE: float

tau_m

The time constant \(\tau_m\) of the first moment, in seconds.

TYPE: float

tau_v

The time constant \(\tau_v\) of the second moment, in seconds.

TYPE: float

eps

The \(\varepsilon\) added to \(\sqrt{\hat v}\). It is > 0, so that an element whose gradient has been 0 does not become 0 / 0.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 1e-08

weight_decay

The decoupled weight decay \(w\).

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 0.01

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

tau, tau_m, tau_v or eps is not finite and

0, or weight_decay is not finite and >= 0.

docs.title: TimeScaled dataclass
docs.text:
TimeScaled(optimizer: Optimizer, *, scale: float)

Bases: Optimizer

Another optimizer on a time that runs scale times as fast: a step of elapsed seconds is a step of elapsed * scale seconds of optimizer.

With scale \(= c\), SGD, RMSProp and AdamW take each time constant \(\tau\) in a step as \(c\,\Delta t / \tau = \Delta t / (\tau / c)\): this is optimizer with all of its time constants divided by \(c\), up to rounding (an optimizer of your own too, if it uses elapsed only as elapsed / tau). weight_decay has no unit and stays as it is: the decay, of the time constant \(\tau / w\), speeds up with \(\tau\).

It is for one stream shown as batches of \(c\) consecutive samples, each batch for as long as one sample: each second of the run then covers \(c\) seconds of the stream, and the time constants of optimizer are written in the stream's seconds. Wrap the optimizer of every node that learns with the same scale. It scales the time of the weights only; the relaxation of r and lam of each sample runs on the run's time, as before. It converts the time and nothing else: the gradient is still the mean over the batch, so the moments of RMSProp and AdamW are those of the mean gradient, whose noise has a variance \(c\) times smaller than that of one sample; a step of theirs is then at least about as large as the sum of \(c\) steps of one sample: about as large when the mean gradient dominates, and up to about \(\sqrt{c}\) times as large when the noise dominates.

The state (state_dict()) is that of optimizer's bound optimizer, with nothing added.

Example (a stream of one sample per 32 ms, shown as batches of 8 consecutive samples, each batch for 32 ms; the time constants are lr=1e-3 and betas=(0.9, 0.999) of torch for one step per sample of the stream)::

optimizer = pc.optim.TimeScaled(
    pc.optim.AdamW(tau=0.032 / 1e-3, tau_m=0.3, tau_v=32.0), scale=8
)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION optimizer

The optimizer that moves the parameters.

TYPE: Optimizer

scale

How many seconds of optimizer's time pass in a second of the run. Keyword only.

TYPE: float

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

scale is not finite and > 0.

docs.title: mujou.pc.relax
docs.text:
The relaxers that move the deviation r = h - mu of a node in time: Euler, or one of your own.

A relaxer is a setting (Relaxer), as an optimizer is: a frozen value that holds no state and may be shared by every node. A node binds it to its own deviation with bind(r), which returns the BoundRelaxer that holds the state (if the relaxer has one) and moves r by step_(r, force, dt, tau_h). It is the counterpart of pc.optim.SGD and pc.optim.AdamW for r: those move the parameters along their gradient, a relaxer moves the deviation along the force on it, \(F = (1 + \tau_h / \tau_r)\,r + \lambda + g\) (functional.relax_). The dual lam is not a relaxer's business: it follows the moved r.

A relaxer changes how r gets to its fixed point, not where it is: at the fixed point the force is zero and the state of the relaxer is at rest, and r stays there.

docs.title: Relaxer
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

The setting of how the deviation r = h - mu of a node moves in time.

It holds values only, no state, so the nodes may share it. bind(r) makes the BoundRelaxer of the deviation of one node, which holds the state.

A relaxer of your own inherits this class, and its bound relaxer BoundRelaxer, and implements every abstract method of both: a class that misses one raises TypeError when it is instantiated (as any abc.ABC). For example, a step that is capped in size::

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Capped(pc.relax.Relaxer):
    limit: float

    def bind(self, r):
        return _BoundCapped(self.limit)

class _BoundCapped(pc.relax.BoundRelaxer):
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self._limit = limit

    def step_(self, r, force, dt, tau_h):
        step = (dt / tau_h) * force
        r.sub_(step.clamp(-self._limit, self._limit))

    def reset_(self, samples):
        pass

    def state_dict(self):
        return {}

    def load_state_dict(self, state):
        pass

Its fixed point must be a zero of the force (with the state of the relaxer at rest), or the node no longer solves PC-ALM: lam is the credit of backpropagation only where r stops at a zero of the force.

docs.text:

docs.title: BoundRelaxer
docs.text:
Bases: Stateful

A relaxer bound to the deviation r of one node, which holds its state.

The node that bound it owns it and calls it from its own hooks only. It is a Stateful, so an attribute of a node that holds it is in the node's state by itself: state_dict returns the state with tensors that share memory with the relaxer's, and load_state_dict copies the tensors of the state into those. Only step_ moves r.

docs.text:
step_(r: Tensor, force: Tensor, dt: float, tau_h: float) -> None

Move r in place by dt seconds of the flow along force, without recording gradients.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION r

force

The time to move by, in seconds (0 changes nothing).

tau_h

The time constant \(\tau_h\) of r, in seconds (TimeConstants.h).

docs.title: reset_ abstractmethod
docs.text:
reset_(samples: Tensor) -> None

Forget the state of samples (batch bool), whose r the node has just set to zero: the node calls it when it first sees a sample whose reset is set, where what the relaxer remembers is of the sample before. A relaxer without memory does nothing.

It is not called when the prediction jumps (the weights or the input change): neither r nor the force jumps then.

The plain gradient flow of r, \(\tau_h \dot r = -F\), by one explicit Euler step of dt: r -= (dt / tau_h) * force.

It is the default. The bound relaxer has no state (an empty state_dict).

hidden = pc.Layer(module, act_spec=..., tau=tau, optimizer=...,
                  relaxer=pc.relax.Euler(), learn_interval=24e-3)

docs.text:
The losses of each sample for an output node.

A loss takes the prediction y_hat and the target y and returns the loss of each sample, of the shape of the batch. The node sums them; it never averages over the batch, so that the gradient it sends to the previous node is the credit of each sample (specs/pc.md). Each class holds its batch for the functions of functional of the same name.

Example::

loss = pc.loss.MSELoss()  # one sample: y_hat (out,) -> ()
loss = pc.loss.MSELoss(64)  # y_hat (64, out) -> (64,)

The batch that the shapes start with; () for one sample.

loss = pc.loss.CrossEntropyLoss(64)  # y_hat (64, C), y (64,) -> (64,)

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
Bases: TypedDict

The activity a node sends to the next nodes, with the target of each of its samples.

The tensors start with the batch, batch: () for one sample, (B,) for B samples, or more dimensions (see activity_spec).

  • h: the activity, (*batch, *out).
  • y: the target of each sample, (*batch, *target).
  • mask: batch bool, whether each sample has a target. A sample whose mask is False adds nothing to the loss, whatever its y is.
  • reset: batch bool, whether each sample starts anew: a node that first sees the activity sets the state it holds for those samples to zero (r and lam of a Layer). A sample that continues the one before it, as the next frame of a stream does, keeps it.
  • time: the Timestamp that Run.write returned for the input h was computed from; Timestamp(ns=0) before the host first writes.

y, mask, reset and time come from the Sample the host wrote, and every node passes them on with the h it computed from it, in the same message: the output node pairs each prediction with its own target, however fast the host writes.
