docs.title: activity_spec
docs.text:
activity_spec(h: TensorSpec, y: TensorSpec, batch: Size = ()) -> DictSpec[Activity]

Return the spec of an Activity whose h is of the spec h, whose targets are of the spec y and whose samples are batch.

batch is the shape that h and y start with, and that of mask: () (the default) for one sample, B or (B,) for B samples, or more dimensions, such as (E, A) for A agents in each of E environments. The samples must be independent of each other (Layer); a dimension that a module mixes, such as the time of a sequence, belongs to h, not to the batch.

Two calls with equal arguments return equal specs. A node of your own that connects to the nodes of mujou.pc declares its ports with it, or with the act_spec of the node before.

Example::

act = pc.msg.activity_spec(TensorSpec((256,)), TensorSpec((), torch.int64))
act = pc.msg.activity_spec(
    TensorSpec((64, 256)), TensorSpec((64,), torch.int64), batch=64
)
RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

h or y does not start with batch.

docs.title: mujou.pc.clock
docs.text: When a node that learns updates its parameters: LearnClock and the Tick it returns for each update.

docs.title: LearnClock
docs.text:
LearnClock(*, period: float, learn_interval: float | None, max_dt: float)

Bases: Stateful

Decides, update by update, when a node updates its parameters, from the time the host wrote the node's input.

The node calls tick(dt, time, now) once in each update, with the dt of the update, the Timestamp the input it received was written at, and the time now on the run's timer. The clock learns in the first update at or after time + k * learn_interval (k = 1, 2, ...), but never in the update that first sees an input: its gradient is still that of the input before. The nodes on a path read the one timer of the run, so they learn at about the same time, however deep they are. With learn_interval=None, it learns in every update, a new input or not; with math.inf, never.

A Tick with learn counts as learned: the next interval starts there, whether the node updates its parameters or skips them for want of a target. elapsed sums the capped dt since then; an input that changes before the clock learned from it drops that sum, as an input without a target does, or inputs that change faster than learn_interval would pile the time up into one large update. dt is capped at max_dt, and the time beyond it is dropped from elapsed too.

The clock starts as if it had seen no input (no time a host writes at): the first update sees a new input, also one written at time 0.

The state (state_dict()) holds the time of the input seen last ("seen_ns", None before any), the time from which the next update learns ("learn_at_ns"), "elapsed", and whether the clock has learned since the input changed ("learned_input"). An attribute of a node that holds a LearnClock is in the node's state by itself.

It is not tied to PC-ALM: any node that learns from inputs the host writes can use it. LearnClock.of makes the clock of a node of PC-ALM from its time constants.

Example::

self.clock = pc.clock.LearnClock(period=self.period, learn_interval=24e-3,
                           max_dt=2e-3)
# In on_update(dt):
tick = self.clock.tick(dt, activity["time"], self.timer.now())
# ... move by tick.dt; if tick.learn, learn weighted by tick.elapsed.
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION period

The period of the node, in seconds.

TYPE: float

learn_interval

The time in seconds from the write of an input to the first update of the parameters, and between the updates while the input stays. None learns in every update, math.inf never.

TYPE: float | None

max_dt

The longest dt an update counts, in seconds.

TYPE: float

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

learn_interval is neither None nor > 0, max_dt is not > 0, or period is longer than max_dt.

docs.title: mujou.pc.functional
docs.text:
The stateless computations of PC-ALM that the nodes of mujou.pc are made of, for writing nodes of your own (such as one with several inputs).

A node i predicts mu = f(h_in; theta) from the activity h_in of the previous node, and keeps the deviation r = h - mu of its activity h and the dual lam of the constraint h = mu. Its energy is E = 0.5 * ||r + lam||^2 (delta = r + lam).

  • vjp gives the gradients of E with respect to h_in and theta (one vector-Jacobian product inside the node). The node sends the one of h_in to the previous node, which adds the values it receives into its g.
  • loss_vjp does the same for an output node, whose energy is the loss.
  • relax_ moves r and lam by dt seconds (r as a relaxer of mujou.pc.relax says: pc.relax.Euler or one of your own); an optimizer of mujou.pc.optim (pc.optim.SGD, pc.optim.AdamW) moves theta.
  • mse and cross_entropy are losses of each sample, for loss_vjp (MSELoss and CrossEntropyLoss hold their batch).

Every g here is a gradient of an energy; the update subtracts it. Gradients are summed over the batch, and the 1 / B (B the number of samples) is applied to theta only (the node divides g_theta by B before it gives it to the optimizer), so lam holds the credit of each sample. The shapes start with the batch, batch (see activity_spec).

docs.title: vjp
docs.text:
vjp(
    module: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor],
    h_in: Tensor,
    delta: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor],
    params: Sequence[Tensor] = (),
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, list[torch.Tensor]]

Predict mu = module(h_in) and the gradients of the node's energy.

With the activity \(h\) held fixed, the energy \(E = \tfrac12\|h - \mu + \lambda\|^2\) has the gradients

\[ g_{\mathrm{in}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial h_{\mathrm{in}}} = -J_h^\top \delta,\qquad g_\theta = \frac{\partial E}{\partial \theta} = -J_\theta^\top \delta, \]

where \(\delta = h - \mu + \lambda\) and \(J\) are the Jacobians of module at h_in. Both are summed over the batch. h_in is detached first, so no graph reaches the node that sent it.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION module

The function f of the node, (*batch, *in) -> (*batch, *out). It must treat the samples independently.

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor]

h_in

The activity of the previous node, (*batch, *in).

TYPE: Tensor

delta

Makes \(\delta\) of the node, (*batch, *out), from mu (detached, without gradients), such as lambda mu: r + lam.

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor]

params

The parameters to get the gradients of, usually those of module that require gradients.

TYPE: Sequence[Tensor] DEFAULT: ()

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Tensor

(mu, g_in, g_theta): mu ((*batch, *out), detached), g_in

Tensor

((*batch, *in)) and g_theta (one tensor per parameter, in the order of

list[Tensor]

params; a parameter that module does not use gets zeros).

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

delta does not make a tensor of the shape of mu.

docs.title: loss_vjp
docs.text:
loss_vjp(
    module: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor],
    h_in: Tensor,
    y: Tensor,
    mask: Tensor,
    loss: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor],
    params: Sequence[Tensor] = (),
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, list[torch.Tensor]]

Predict y_hat = module(h_in) and the gradients of the masked loss.

The energy of an output node is the loss of the samples that have a target,

\[ \ell = \sum_b \mathrm{mask}_b\, \ell_b(\hat y_b, y_b),\qquad g_{\mathrm{in}} = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial h_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad g_\theta = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta}. \]

A sample whose mask is False adds nothing, whatever its y is (NaN too): its y is replaced by zeros before loss sees it, and its g_in is \(J^\top 0\), zero as long as its y_hat is finite (NaN where it is not). With every mask False, g_in is thus zeros. h_in is detached first.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION module

The function f of the node, (*batch, *in) -> (*batch, *out).

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor]

h_in

The activity of the previous node, (*batch, *in).

TYPE: Tensor

y

The target, (*batch, *target).

TYPE: Tensor

mask

Whether each sample has a target, batch bool.

TYPE: Tensor

loss

The loss of each sample, (y_hat, y) -> batch, such as MSELoss(batch) or CrossEntropyLoss(batch).

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor]

params

The parameters to get the gradients of.

TYPE: Sequence[Tensor] DEFAULT: ()

RETURNS DESCRIPTION tuple[Tensor, Tensor, list[Tensor]]

(y_hat, g_in, g_theta) as vjp returns (mu, g_in, g_theta).

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

loss does not return the shape of mask, as a loss that averages over the batch (nn.MSELoss()) does.

docs.title: relax_
docs.text:
relax_(
    r: Tensor,
    lam: Tensor,
    g: Tensor,
    dt: float,
    tau: TimeConstants,
    relaxer: BoundRelaxer | None = None,
) -> None

Move r and lam in place by one explicit Euler step of dt seconds of

\[ \tau_h \dot r = -(r + \lambda + g) - \frac{\tau_h}{\tau_r}\,r,\qquad \tau_\lambda \dot\lambda = r. \]

r = h - mu is the deviation of the node's activity from its prediction, which stays in the node: the node sends mu. The step moves r first and then lam with the moved r. g is held fixed. The step is not split: g comes from the next nodes and stays as it was over dt, so the coupling between the nodes is explicit however finely the step is split. Keep dt short instead (Layer caps it at max_dt). tau.lam = inf leaves lam exactly as it is, and tau.r = inf adds no decay.

With a relaxer (pc.relax.Euler().bind(r) or one of your own), r moves as it says along the force \(F = (1 + \tau_h / \tau_r)\,r + \lambda + g\) instead of by the plain step: relaxer.step_(r, F, dt, tau.h). \(\lambda\) follows the moved r as before. The relaxer is the node's: it holds the state, and the node calls its reset_ where the force jumps.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION r

The deviation h - mu of the node, (*batch, *out).

TYPE: Tensor

lam

The dual of the node's activity, (*batch, *out).

TYPE: Tensor

g

The sum of the gradients the next nodes sent, (*batch, *out).

TYPE: Tensor

dt

The time to move by, in seconds.

TYPE: float

tau

The time constants of r and lam.

TYPE: TimeConstants

relaxer

How r moves, bound to r; None is the plain step.

TYPE: BoundRelaxer | None DEFAULT: None

docs.title: mse
docs.text:
mse(y_hat: Tensor, y: Tensor, batch: Size = ()) -> torch.Tensor

Return the mean squared error of each sample of batch.

The squared error is averaged over the dimensions of a sample, as nn.MSELoss averages it, but not over the batch: the mean of the result is nn.MSELoss()(y_hat, y), and with the 1 / B the node applies before its optimizer, theta follows its gradient.

With d values in a sample, its gradient with respect to y_hat is (2 / d) * (y_hat - y): that of 0.5 * ||y - y_hat||^2 for d = 2, twice it for d = 1. The larger it is, the more strongly the output pulls on the activities, and the shorter the period that keeps their explicit steps stable; for a scalar target, a loss of your own such as 0.5 * mse(y_hat, y, batch) keeps the pull of the half.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION y_hat

The prediction, (*batch, *out).

TYPE: Tensor

y

The target, of the same shape as y_hat.

TYPE: Tensor

batch

The batch that the shapes start with; () for one sample.

TYPE: Size DEFAULT: ()

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Tensor

The loss of each sample, batch.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

The shapes differ (a broadcast would silently give another shape), or they do not start with batch.

docs.title: cross_entropy
docs.text:
cross_entropy(y_hat: Tensor, y: Tensor, batch: Size = ()) -> torch.Tensor

Return the cross entropy of each sample of batch.

The classes are the dimension right after the batch, as in F.cross_entropy ((N, C) and (C,) alike). A sample with more dimensions, such as one class for each pixel ((*batch, C, H, W)), has its cross entropy averaged over them, as nn.CrossEntropyLoss does, but not over the batch: the mean of the result is nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(y_hat, y). A class of -100 (the ignore_index of torch) adds zero but still counts in that mean; leave a sample out with mask instead.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION y_hat

The logits, (*batch, C, *rest).

TYPE: Tensor

y

The class of each sample, (*batch, *rest) int64, or the probability of each class, of the shape of y_hat.

TYPE: Tensor

batch

The batch that the shapes start with; () for one sample.

TYPE: Size DEFAULT: ()

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Tensor

The loss of each sample, batch.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

y_hat or y does not start with batch.

docs.title: mujou.run
docs.text:
run(
    root: Node | Network,
    *,
    timer: Timer | None = None,
    inputs: Mapping[P, Message] | None = None,
    state: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    workers: int | None = None,
) -> Run

Run root, a node or a network, in the background; return once every node has started.

The nodes are at their paths from the root: those of a network at "l1", "body.l1", ..., and a node given as the root at "". To run several side by side, put them in a Group. The host writes and reads the ports themselves (run.write({node.prev: x})).

Every node's on_start (and, with state, the node's load_state_dict) has returned, and the run's timer runs when this returns. A node runs once: run new instances to run again (the attributes of the nodes of a run stay readable after it). A run refused before any node started (by any error but NetworkError) has changed nothing, and the same instances run once the cause is fixed.

The run's nodes share a pool of workers threads, which it creates for itself; a node with dedicated_thread=True runs on a thread of its own instead. A worker runs one hook of one node at a time, the updates that are due earliest first. A hook that blocks holds its worker, so the other nodes' dt grows meanwhile.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION root

The node or network to run.

TYPE: Node | Network

timer

The time axis of the run: every node's dt, every message's time and every pause of the run is on it. None is mujou.time.global_timer, which every run without a timer of its own shares.

TYPE: Timer | None DEFAULT: None

inputs

The initial values of unconnected ports that receive, as Run.write takes them (and copies them, to the same places), written when the run starts. Written after state, they replace its values. They bear the time of the run's timer when the run starts (with state, the time of the tree).

TYPE: Mapping[P, Message] | None DEFAULT: None

state

A tree from Run.state_dict to restore. The slots, the nodes' states (through each node's load_state_dict, after its on_start) and their last update times continue from the time the tree was taken, on a new Timer of the run's own that starts at that time and time scale (so global_timer and the other runs do not move, and a pause of global_timer does not pause it). Build the tree to run as the one the tree came from: the same node paths, ports and peers.

TYPE: Mapping[str, Any] | None DEFAULT: None

workers

The number of worker threads of the run (>= 1). None is as many as the CPUs the process may use (the logical cores, or fewer when the CPU affinity or a quota limits them), or half of them (at least 1) while the GIL is enabled at run time (sys._is_gil_enabled()), never more than the nodes on the workers. With no such node, the run has no worker.

TYPE: int | None DEFAULT: None

Example, with the node Error of the example of Run::

node = Error()
with mujou.run(node, inputs={node.prev: torch.ones(2)}) as run:
    run.timer.sleep(0.1)
    error = run.read(node.next)
RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

A node of the tree has already run ("Leaky has already run; create a new instance (its attributes stay readable)"); or this is called from a node's hook.

(TypeError, ValueError)

The tree is invalid (as Node and Network say); or inputs or the initial value of a port do not match their specs (as Run.write raises).

ValueError

workers is less than 1; timer and state are both given (a restored run runs on a timer of its own); state does not have the timer, nodes, ports and peers of the tree; or a port of the tree is connected to a port whose node is not in the tree.

NetworkError

A node raised while starting; the run has stopped.

docs.title: mujou.Run
docs.text:
Run(wiring: Wiring, runtime: Runtime, timer: Timer, clock: ReadOnlyTimer)

A run of a tree of nodes, as mujou.run returns it: what the host uses to talk to the running nodes.

The nodes run in the background, on the run's worker threads (or threads of their own); the host's thread only writes inputs, reads outputs and takes the state:

  • write inputs, read / read_with_time / subscribe / wait_for outputs, take a state_dict.
  • shutdown() to stop the run, or join() to wait until it stops.
  • After a normal end: take the final state_dict, and read the nodes' attributes (a module they learned, say).

A with statement shuts the run down at its end. These methods are for the host: calling them from a node's hook raises RuntimeError.

If a node raises, the whole run stops. If that happens while mujou.run starts the nodes, mujou.run raises NetworkError; otherwise every later call of write, read, read_with_time, subscribe (and its iterator), wait_for, state_dict, shutdown, join and ManualRun.step raises it. Its __cause__ is the node's exception. The state at the exception is not kept. A with left by another exception lets that exception through instead.

A run keeps running when the host drops it, until shutdown or, at the latest, the interpreter's exit: once the non-daemon threads have ended, the exit shuts down every run still running and waits for their on_stop. A thread that iterates over subscribe keeps the exit waiting until its run ends, so shut the run down before the program ends (with does).

mujou.run and mujou.run_manually make it.

Example::

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import Node, Port, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((2,))


class Error(Node):  # sends its input minus its teacher
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.teacher = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.prev.recv() - self.teacher.recv())


node = Error()
x, y = torch.ones(2), torch.zeros(2)
with mujou.run(node, inputs={node.prev: x, node.teacher: y}) as run:
    run.write({node.prev: 2 * x, node.teacher: x})  # switch together
    run.timer.sleep(0.1)  # present the input for 0.1 s of the run's time
    error, t = run.read_with_time(node.next)
state = run.state_dict()  # the state at the end, to save

docs.title: timer property
docs.text:
timer: Timer

The run's timer: the timer given to mujou.run, mujou.time.global_timer when none was given, or, for a run restored from a state, a new Timer that started at the time of the state.

Every node's dt and every time of the run is on it. The host waits, pauses and scales the time of the run with it.

docs.title: write
docs.text:
write(values: Mapping[P, Message]) -> Timestamp

Write messages to unconnected ports that receive, and return the time they are stamped with.

The values are detached and copied. A dense tensor on the CUDA device of the port's node is copied on that device, on this thread's current stream of it, which write waits for; any other tensor is copied to host memory (so a node on another device or on the CPU never waits for what this thread queues on a GPU). The nodes receive the values on their own devices. All of them switch together and bear the same time: at any one moment, a node sees either all of them or none. (A node that reads two of them one after the other may still see a later write in between; compare the times to tell.) Any such port of the run can be written, exposed by the root or not.

The time is the run's timer at the write, as a node's recv_with_time and the "in" slots of state_dict show it; read_with_time shows the times of sends, not of writes. An empty values changes nothing and returns the time all the same.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

The run has stopped normally (no node reads what is written then).

ValueError

A port is not an unconnected Port of this run that receives; or a shape or a dtype differs from the spec.

TypeError

A value is not of its field's kind (a tensor, an int, ...), or a dict message does not have the spec's keys.

OverflowError

An int is out of the range of its IntSpec.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: read
docs.text:
read(port: Port[S, Any] | MultiPort[S, Any]) -> S

Return the latest message port sent.

Any port of the run that sends can be read, so a connected port shows an inner node. Only send (to every peer, not MultiPort.send_to) updates the value read here; before the first one it is the port's initial (zeros by default) or the value restored from state. The tensors are new copies on the CPU. read_with_time also returns the time it was sent at.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

port is not a port of this run that sends.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: read_with_time
docs.text:
read_with_time(port: Port[S, Any] | MultiPort[S, Any]) -> tuple[S, Timestamp | None]

Return the latest message port sent, as read does, and the time it was sent at: None before the first send (the port's initial, or the restored value of a port that had not sent).

The time is on the run's timer. A Timestamp does not say which timer it is on: compare it only with times of the same timer (run.timer).

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

As read raises.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: subscribe
docs.text:
subscribe(
    port: Port[S, Any] | MultiPort[S, Any], *, timeout: float = math.inf
) -> Iterator[tuple[S, Timestamp | None]]

Iterate over the messages port sends, with their times.

The first step yields the latest message at the time of this call without waiting (before the first send, the port's initial or the restored value, with the time read_with_time gives it). Each later step waits until a newer message is sent and yields the latest; messages sent in between are skipped. Only the consumer waits: the sending node never does. The iterator ends when the run shuts down normally. Without a timeout, a thread iterating here ends only with the run. In a ManualRun nothing is sent unless step is called, so a wait here without a timeout on the thread that steps never ends.

To wait for one message that meets a condition, use wait_for.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION port

The port to follow.

TYPE: Port[S, Any] | MultiPort[S, Any]

timeout

Real (wall-clock) seconds, counted from this call, that the whole iteration may take, the time spent in the loop's body included. math.inf iterates as long as the run runs.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: inf

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

As read raises.

TimeoutError

From the iterator, at a step after the first that begins once timeout has passed, or that would wait past it. The iterator ends; the run keeps running.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised (also from the iterator).

docs.title: wait_for
docs.text:
wait_for(
    port: Port[S, Any] | MultiPort[S, Any],
    until: Callable[[S], bool],
    *,
    timeout: float = math.inf,
) -> tuple[S, Timestamp | None]

Wait until port sends a message that meets until, and return it with its time (None if the message that meets it is the one before the first send, as read_with_time gives it).

Checks the latest message first, then each newer one as subscribe yields them (messages sent in between are skipped). Only the host waits: the nodes never do. In a ManualRun nothing is sent unless step is called, so a wait without a timeout on the thread that steps never ends. Here with the node Error of the example of Run::

node = Error()
x = torch.ones(2)
with mujou.run(node, inputs={node.prev: x}) as run:
    error, t = run.wait_for(
        node.next, lambda e: torch.equal(e, x), timeout=5.0
    )
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION port

The port to follow.

TYPE: Port[S, Any] | MultiPort[S, Any]

until

Called on each message on the host's thread; True ends the wait.

TYPE: Callable[[S], bool]

timeout

Real (wall-clock) seconds, counted from this call, to wait at most. math.inf waits as long as the run runs.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: inf

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

As read raises.

TimeoutError

timeout passed first. The run keeps running.

RuntimeError

The run shut down normally first.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: state_dict
docs.text:
state_dict(*, timeout: float = math.inf) -> dict[str, Any]

Copy the state of the run at one time, while it runs or after it ended normally.

While it runs, this pauses the run's timer and nodes, copies the state and resumes, and returns once the run has resumed. It waits at most timeout for every node to pause. After a normal end, this copies the state as the nodes left it, calling each node's state_dict on this thread. The tree's timer holds the time at which the run was asked to stop, as if the run had paused then: no update or message of the run is later, though its time scale is the timer's when the state is taken. A run restored from it goes on from there, without the time that passed after the end.

The tree is a plain dict of copies on the CPU (later updates of the nodes do not change it): save it with torch.save, load it with torch.load (weights_only=True reads it), and pass it to mujou.run(..., state=tree) to restore it::

{
    "timer": {"time_ns": int, "time_scale": float},
    "nodes": {
        "body.l1": {
            "state": ...,  # the node's state_dict()
            "last_update_ns": int,
            "ports": {
                "prev": {"in": E},
                "next": {"out": E, "to": {"body.l2.prev": E}},
            },
        },
        ...,
    },
}

A node is keyed by its path from the root ("" for a node that is the root itself), and each of its ports by its attribute. A port that sends has "out", its latest message (what read returns), and "to", its latest message to each peer (MultiPort.send_to writes only one), by the path of the peer's port. An unconnected Port that receives has "in", what the host wrote last. Each E is {"value": message, "time_ns": int | None}: time_ns is None while nothing was written. As every time of the tree, a Timestamp in a message (a TimestampSpec) is held as its nanoseconds, an int.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION timeout

Real (wall-clock) seconds to wait for every node to pause (the end of its current on_update). math.inf waits as long as it takes.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: inf

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

This is called from a node's hook.

TimeoutError

A node did not pause within timeout; no state is taken and the run keeps running.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised (its state is not kept).

Exception

After a normal end, what a node's state_dict raised; the run stays ended normally.

docs.title: shutdown
docs.text:
shutdown(*, timeout: float = math.inf) -> None

Stop every node and return once every on_stop has returned.

Does nothing after a normal end.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION timeout

Real (wall-clock) seconds to wait for the end. math.inf waits as long as it takes.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: inf

RAISES DESCRIPTION TimeoutError

The run did not stop within timeout. The stop stays asked: the nodes take no more updates and the run goes on stopping in the background (an on_stop may still be running). join waits for the end.

ValueError

timeout is negative or NaN; nothing changes.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

join(*, timeout: float = math.inf) -> None

Wait until the run stops, without asking it to stop.

It returns once another thread called shutdown and every on_stop has returned; if a node raises, it raises instead. If nothing stops the run and timeout is math.inf, it never returns.

docs.title: mujou.run_manually
docs.text:
run_manually(
    root: Node | Network,
    *,
    timer: VirtualTimer | None = None,
    inputs: Mapping[P, Message] | None = None,
    state: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    workers: int | None = None,
) -> ManualRun

Run root as mujou.run does, with the nodes updating only when ManualRun.step lets them, for simulations and tests.

mujou.run runs in real time, for deploying to the real world; mujou.run_manually runs in virtual time, for simulating as fast as the machine computes. Each update sees as its dt the time stepped since the node's last update, and with deterministic nodes that share no Python objects the result is the same, bit for bit, every time.

The default timer is a new mujou.time.VirtualTimer at time 0 (with state, at the time of the state), which ManualRun.timer returns and ManualRun.step advances. Pass a VirtualTimer of your own to share it between runs: a step of one then moves the time of the others too.

inputs, state and workers are those of mujou.run (the workers run the updates of a step in parallel), and so are the errors.

Example::

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import Node, Port, TensorSpec


class Double(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = Port(recv=TensorSpec((2,)))
        self.next = Port(send=TensorSpec((2,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(2 * self.prev.recv())


class Chain(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = Double(), Double()
        self.a.next.connect(self.b.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.a.prev, self.b.next


net = Chain()
x = torch.ones(2)
with mujou.run_manually(net, inputs={net.prev: x}) as run:
    run.step(0.001, net.a, net.b)  # 1 ms later, a, then b reads a's value
    y, t = run.read_with_time(net.next)
assert torch.equal(y, 4 * x) and t is not None and t.ns == 1_000_000
RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

A node of the tree has already run; or this is called from a node's hook.

(TypeError, ValueError)

The tree is invalid; or inputs or the initial value of a port do not match their specs.

ValueError

workers is less than 1; timer and state are both given; or state does not have the timer, nodes, ports and peers of the tree.

NetworkError

A node raised while starting; the run has stopped.

docs.title: mujou.ManualRun
docs.text:
ManualRun(wiring: Wiring, runtime: Runtime, timer: VirtualTimer, clock: ReadOnlyTimer)

Bases: Run

A run whose nodes update only when step lets them, for simulations and tests.

mujou.run_manually returns it. The nodes start and stop as in any run, but between updates each waits for step, which advances the run's VirtualTimer first: every dt is made of the times that were stepped, and with deterministic nodes that share no Python objects the result is the same, bit for bit, every time. Use it to simulate a network as fast as the machine computes, and to test nodes against the discrete algorithm of the chosen order.

docs.title: timer property
docs.text:
timer: VirtualTimer

The run's timer: the VirtualTimer that mujou.run_manually made, or the one given to it.

docs.title: step
docs.text:
step(dt: float, *nodes: Node) -> None

Advance the timer by dt seconds, then update the nodes once each, and return when done.

Without nodes, every node updates at once, in parallel on the run's workers and dedicated threads. Each reads the values from the start of the step: what the nodes send in this step becomes visible to all of them once every update has ended (Jacobi). The result does not depend on the number of workers or on which thread runs which node. While such a step runs, the host reading a port from another thread gets its value from before the step.

With nodes, only they update, one after another in the given order, and a later node reads what an earlier one sent in this step (Gauss-Seidel); what each sends becomes visible once its update has ended. This is not the same as step(dt) in general, even when every node is given. When the messages between different nodes flow without a cycle, updating each receiver before its senders (a chain from the output side back to the input side, for one) gives the result of step(dt); when values also flow back, no order does in general.

Either way, a node does not read in its update what it sent there itself, through a port connected to its own. The period of the nodes does not apply. Each dt a node sees is the time since its last update, the first one from the start of the run (or the last update restored). A node given twice in one step updates once: the second time, its time has not moved. Likewise step(0) right after the start of the run updates no node. The messages sent in a step bear the time of the step. A timer shared with other runs moves for them too. Write inputs between steps.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

A node is not in this run, or dt is negative or not finite.

RuntimeError

The run has stopped normally, the timer is paused, or this is called from a node's hook.

NetworkError

A node raised; the run has stopped. Without nodes, what the nodes sent in that step is not published.

docs.title: mujou.NetworkError
docs.text:
Bases: RuntimeError

The network stopped because a node raised.

__cause__ is the first exception a node raised. Every exception of a hook is logged to logging.getLogger("mujou") at ERROR, with the node's path, the hook and the traceback; those that other nodes raise about the same time are only logged. Once a run has stopped this way, the host's calls on it (write, read, state_dict, shutdown, ...) raise NetworkError too.

docs.title: mujou.time
docs.text:
The time of mujou.

Every run measures its nodes' dt on one timer, a time axis that can be scaled and paused. By default every run shares global_timer; give a run a Timer of its own with mujou.run(..., timer=...). The host controls the time of a run through run.timer, and a node reads it with self.timer.

  • Timer: a time axis, running with the real clock at a scale
  • VirtualTimer: a Timer that moves only when advanced, for tests
  • ReadOnlyTimer: the reading side of a timer, as a node sees its run's timer (Node.timer)
  • Timestamp: a time on a timer, as Run.read_with_time and Port.recv_with_time give it
  • global_timer: the timer of every run not given one of its own

Durations are in seconds of the timer (sleep, advance, dt, period), except timeouts, which are in real seconds. Only the host controls the time: sleep, pause, resume, set_time_scale and VirtualTimer.advance raise RuntimeError in a node's hook.

docs.title: global_timer module-attribute
docs.text:
global_timer: Final[Timer] = Timer(now=Timestamp(ns=14336723))

A time axis that a run's nodes measure their dt on.

Timer() starts at start and runs with the real clock, time_scale seconds of the timer per real second. Give it to mujou.run(..., timer=...) to run a network on a time of its own: a pause of that run (as Run.state_dict takes) then stops only this timer, not global_timer, which every other run uses by default. Every time of the run is a Timestamp on it.

Only the host controls a timer: sleep, pause, resume, set_time_scale (and VirtualTimer.advance) raise RuntimeError in a node's hook, where a node would wait for, or change the dt of, the other nodes. A node reads the time of its run with self.timer.

pause stops the time of every run on the timer at one time T until resume. Take the states of several runs on one timer while it is paused, so that all of them are of the same time T.

The time is held in nanoseconds and saturates at about 584 years.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

time_scale is not finite and > 0.

docs.title: One node's exception stops everything
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    E["A hook of a node raises<br/>(on_update, on_start, state_dict or any other)"] --> L["Logged"]
    L --> X["Each node finishes its running hook, stops, and calls on_exception()<br/>without waiting for the others; the nodes that did not raise too"]
    X -->|"once every on_exception() has returned"| S["on_stop() on every node<br/>the one that raised included"]
    E --> H["The host gets NetworkError<br/>__cause__ is the first exception"]
"""What happens when a node raises.

The whole run stops: every node's ``on_exception``, then its ``on_stop``, is
called, and the host gets a ``NetworkError`` whose ``__cause__`` is the node's
exception. An exception in ``on_start`` comes from ``mujou.run`` itself.
"""

import logging
import sys
from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NetworkError, Node, Port, TensorSpec

SCALAR = TensorSpec(())

# mujou also logs the node's exception, with its traceback, to the "mujou" logger.
# Show the log on stdout here (without a handler, Python prints it to stderr).
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="log: %(message)s")


class Checked(Node):
    """Passes its input on, and raises once it is negative."""

    def __init__(self, fail_on_start: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fail_on_start = fail_on_start
        self.prev = Port(recv=SCALAR)
        self.next = Port(send=SCALAR)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        if self.fail_on_start:
            raise RuntimeError("cannot start")

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        u = self.prev.recv()
        if u < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"negative input: {u.item()}")
        self.next.send(u)

    @override
    def on_exception(self) -> None:
        super().on_exception()
        print("on_exception: called on every node")

    @override
    def on_stop(self) -> None:
        super().on_stop()
        print("on_stop: called after on_exception")


class Single(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self, fail_on_start: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.checked = Checked(fail_on_start)
        self.prev = self.checked.prev


# An exception while the run goes on reaches the host at its next call.
net = Single()
run = mujou.run(net)
run.write({net.prev: torch.tensor(-1.0)})
try:
    run.join(timeout=10.0)  # waits until the run stops (here: by the exception)
except NetworkError as error:
    cause = error.__cause__
    print(f"NetworkError, caused by {type(cause).__name__}: {cause}")
    assert isinstance(cause, ValueError)

# An exception in on_start comes from mujou.run.
try:
    mujou.run(Single(fail_on_start=True))
except NetworkError as error:
    print(f"mujou.run raised NetworkError, caused by {error.__cause__!r}")
    assert isinstance(error.__cause__, RuntimeError)
Why not stop only the node that raised?

Its neighbors would keep reading its old values and drift away from the equilibrium without anyone noticing.

docs.title: Where the host receives it
docs.text:
An exception while the run starts (on_start, ...) is raised by mujou.run; one after the start, by the host's next call of a Run method, as NetworkError. So a host that only waits waits with run.join(timeout=...), not with run.timer.sleep.

AvoidWrite instead 
run = mujou.run(net)
run.timer.sleep(10.0)  # does not notice when a node raises

run = mujou.run(net)
run.join(timeout=10.0)  # a node's exception arrives as NetworkError (TimeoutError if it has not stopped in 10 s)

docs.title: on_exception and on_stop
docs.text:
Hook What to write on_exception() The work of an abnormal end, such as a safe stop of the actuators on_stop() The release of resources such as I/O; called at every end

on_exception takes no arguments, so a node does not learn what stopped the run; the host handles the cause, from the __cause__ of NetworkError. To handle an exception in the node, catch it with try in the hook (an exception caught there does not stop the run).

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: A node's exception is logged with its traceback (the logger's name and level are in NetworkError). Configure Python's logging to send it elsewhere: the logging.basicConfig line of the program above sends it to standard output (standard error if not configured).

docs.title: The state after an exception
docs.text: The state of a run that ended by an exception is not kept, so take the state you want to keep while it runs (regularly in a long run), and build new instances to run again.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Which seconds the timeout of a waiting call counts is in the table of units of time.

A long on_update delays the pause

A node whose single on_update is long (heavy BP, say) delays every pause for the state, since each node finishes its running on_update before it pauses.

docs.title: Interpreter exit
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant I as Interpreter
    participant T as Other non-daemon threads
    participant M as Mujou
    participant N as Every node
    I->>T: waits for them to end
    Note over T: a thread iterating over subscribe<br/>does not end until its run ends
    I->>M: shut the run down
    M->>N: on_stop()
    N-->>M: every on_stop returns
    M-->>I: done

docs.title: 🗂️ Groups
docs.text: mujou.run runs one root, so to run several networks in one run, put them side by side in a Group. How nodes get their paths is in Networks and paths.

docs.title: Group
docs.text:
# By keyword: two networks connected before they are grouped.
enc, dec = Stage(2.0), Stage(3.0)
enc.next.connect(dec.prev)  # the ports a network exposes, as for nodes
x = torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0])
with mujou.run(Group(enc=enc, dec=dec), inputs={enc.prev: x}) as run:
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes, and how many fit in a given
    # time depends on how the threads get scheduled: follow the output until y
    # arrives (TimeoutError after 5 s).
    # The ports are those of the networks given.
    y, _ = run.wait_for(dec.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 6 * x), timeout=5.0)
    nodes = list(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
print(f"keyword: nodes {nodes}, y = {y}")
assert nodes == ["enc.scale", "dec.scale"]
assert torch.equal(y, 6 * x)

# Two independent networks in one run.
first, second = Stage(2.0), Stage(3.0)
both = Group(first=first, second=second)
with mujou.run(both, inputs={first.prev: x, second.prev: x}) as run:
    y1, _ = run.wait_for(first.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x), timeout=5.0)
    y2, _ = run.wait_for(second.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 3 * x), timeout=5.0)
    nodes = list(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
print(f"side by side: nodes {nodes}, y1 = {y1}, y2 = {y2}")
assert nodes == ["first.scale", "second.scale"]
assert torch.equal(y1, 2 * x) and torch.equal(y2, 3 * x)

docs.text:
The host writes with Run.write only to ports that receive and are not connected (nodes write the others). A written value stays until the next write, and the nodes read it many times. Write values that belong together, such as an input and its target, in one write (why: Values that belong together).

run.write({net.prev: x, net.teacher: y})  # x and y switch together

    run.write({net.prev: x})  # a few updates before this may read zeros

    run.write({net.prev: x})

run's timer → Input Output x₁ x₂ write(x₂) read right after → output for x₁ read after sleep showing time of run.timer.sleep The delay of the output depends on the time constants of the nodes and the number of stages. Show the input long enough

When you know the output to expect, wait for it with wait_for instead of sleeping (Run).

The host reads any port of the run that sends, connected or not. Reading a connected port observes a value in the middle of the network without changing it.

docs.title: subscribe
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant N as Node
    participant H as Host (subscribe)
    Note over H: gets the latest value v0 at once
    N-->>H: send(v1)
    Note over H: gets v1 and handles it
    N-->>H: send(v2)

clock = Clock()  # a node runs by itself, without a network
with mujou.run(clock) as run:
    received: list[tuple[float, float]] = []
    # timeout: give up after 5 s of real time instead of waiting forever.
    for value, t in run.subscribe(clock.next, timeout=5.0):
        if t is None:  # the zeros the port holds until the clock first sends
            continue
        received.append((value.item(), float(t)))
        if len(received) == 20:
            break

docs.text: examples/mnist/ and examples/cifar10/ learn with a pc.Chain and compare it with BP from the same initial weights on the same batches; below are the results, and how the way the network is cut and cuda_graph affect the speed.

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I["input<br/>784"] --> L0["layer0<br/>784 → 256, ReLU"] --> L1["layer1<br/>256 → 256, ReLU"] --> O["output<br/>256 → 10<br/>cross-entropy"]
Result (seed 0) PC-ALM BP Test accuracy after 3 epochs 97.69% 97.53% Prequential accuracy Within 0.11 points of BP in every epoch — Compute time per batch (CPU) About 40 times that of BP — 
uv run python examples/mnist/main.py            # 3 epochs, about 2 minutes

# The learning rate of one batch is shown / optimizer.tau: the nodes learn
# once per batch, for the time since they last learned.

net = pc.Chain(
    *modules,
    x=TensorSpec((args.batch, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((args.batch,), torch.int64),
    batch=args.batch,
    loss=pc.loss.CrossEntropyLoss(args.batch),

    optimizer=optimizer,

with mujou.run(net, timer=timer, workers=args.workers) as run:
    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        right = total = 0
        start = time.perf_counter()
        for i, (x, y, mask) in enumerate(
            batches(data.train_x, data.train_y, args.batch, shuffle(epoch))
        ):
            # Shuffled batches: no sample continues the one before it.
            sample = pc.msg.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=mask, reset=torch.ones_like(mask))
            p = pc.show(run, net, sample, seconds=shown)
            if not torch.isfinite(p["y_hat"]).all():
                raise SystemExit("PC-ALM diverged: lower --time-scale")
            right += correct(p["y_hat"], y, mask)  # before learning from it
            total += int(mask.sum())
            if args.watch and epoch == 0 and i == 100:  # a pause to look
                watch.check(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
        seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
        # Test: the same nodes, with no label to learn from.
        test_right = test_total = 0
        for x, y, mask in batches(data.test_x, data.test_y, args.batch):
            unlabeled = torch.zeros_like(mask)  # keep mask to score with
            p = pc.show(
                run,
                net,
                pc.msg.Sample(
                    x=x, y=y, mask=unlabeled, reset=torch.ones_like(mask)
                ),
                seconds=shown,
            )
            test_right += correct(p["y_hat"], y, mask)
            test_total += int(mask.sum())
        results.append(Epoch(right / total, test_right / test_total, seconds))
        print(
            f"PC-ALM epoch {epoch + 1}: prequential {right / total:.2%}, "
            f"test {test_right / test_total:.2%}, {seconds:.1f} s"
        )
Term or option Meaning Prequential accuracy (in training) Measured on the first prediction for each batch, which pc.show returns. How well the model predicts data it has not seen yet Test accuracy The host shows the test batches with every mask False, so no node learns from them, and keeps the original mask to score with. There is no inference mode to switch to The last batch data.batches pads the last batch with zeros whose mask is False, so that every batch has the size of the specs. Only the samples whose original mask is True are counted --watch Counts the dt of each node (watch.py), and warns when the updates come later than 1.5 periods (median) or 2 periods (99%). At --time-scale 2, 99% of the updates still came within 1.25 periods, with the same accuracy File mnist/ cifar10/ main.py Entry point Entry point data.py Loads the data Loads and augments the data metrics.py Measures Measures bp.py Trains the BP baseline Trains the BP baseline watch.py Counts the dt of the nodes (--watch) — resnet.py — Builds the network and says why it is cut into few nodes

data.py, metrics.py and bp.py do not depend on mujou.pc: the data are plain tensors, and the BP baseline is plain PyTorch.

docs.title: cuda_graph
docs.text:
layer = pc.Layer(stage, act_spec=spec, tau=tau, optimizer=optimizer, learn_interval=learn_interval, device="cuda", cuda_graph=True)

With a small batch on a GPU, an update of a pc.Layer is bound by the CPU launching kernels. cuda_graph=True replays the vector-Jacobian product from a CUDA graph: on a vision stage of a ViT with one sample (an RTX 4090), the product took 0.47 ms instead of 2.06 ms.

docs.title: 🔩 How mujou.pc Works
docs.text: You should know PyTorch and BP, and the nodes and dt of How Mujou Works. You need not know predictive coding. For how to use it, see 5. Learn with PC-ALM; for how to choose the values, PC-ALM; for the theory, the PC-ALM article.

docs.title: How it differs from BP
docs.text: Topic BP in plain PyTorch mujou.pc Inference and learning Forward, backward and optimizer.step(), one by one At the same time. Every node updates on its own period, and learns while the host shows the input. No modes: a sample whose mask is False is not learned from The loss Usually the mean over the batch Output sums the loss of each sample (shaped like the batch) Gradients and the graph .backward() through the whole model Only inside each node (vjp detaches h_in). Neighbors exchange activities and the gradients g_in as messages How the credit travels One backward sweep. A gradient received is multiplied by the VJP and passed straight on The sum g of the g_in received moves the node's own r and lam, and the node sends the g_in of the moved delta. One node per update toward the input. No phases, no waiting, and the latest g at hand (which may be old) Equal to the BP gradient Always Only at equilibrium. That is why a node waits learn_interval before it learns Cost of one batch One forward and one backward Shown for S periods, S forwards and VJPs in each node (measured in the PC-ALM experiments)

docs.title: What a node holds
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    PREV["Previous node"] -->|"h_in (activity, forward)"| F["module<br/>mu = f(h_in; θ)"]
    F -->|"mu (prediction, forward)"| NEXT["Next node"]
    subgraph HOLD["Kept in the node (h = mu + r is not sent)"]
        R["r = h − mu<br/>(deviation)"]
        LAM["lam<br/>(dual)"]
    end
    NEXT -.->|"sum of g_in = g (back)"| R
    R --> D["delta = r + lam"]
    LAM --> D
    D -.->|"g_in = −J_hᵀ delta (back)"| PREV
Quantity Formula Meaning h_in The activity that came from the node before mu \(\mu = f(h_{\mathrm{in}};\theta)\) The prediction: the output of the node's module. \(\theta\) are the weights of module r \(r = h - \mu\) The deviation from the prediction, which the node holds h \(h = \mu + r\) The node's own activity. It stays in the node: the next node reads mu lam \(\tau_\lambda\dot\lambda = r\) The dual: the deviation summed up over time delta \(\delta = r + \lambda\) The node's error g_in \(g_{\mathrm{in}} = -J_h^\top \delta\) The gradient sent back to the node before (\(J_h\) is the Jacobian of module with respect to h_in) g The sum of the g_in that came from the next nodes

At the equilibrium, where both r and lam stop, r = 0, lam is the credit of BP \(-\partial\ell/\partial h\), and the gradients of the weights equal those of BP (pc.Layer).

docs.title: Why the node holds r and sends mu
docs.text:
Choice The article's node: holds h, sends \(\mu + r\) mujou's node: holds r, sends mu When mu jumps h stays, and \(r = h - \mu\) suddenly grows. A false error enters g_in and the weight gradients Keeps the deviation r as it is The activity that flows forward \(\mu + r\) The forward pass mu How the credit flows A loop: a move of r moves the activities of the nodes above and comes back to the node Back only A chain whose forward pass amplifies Diverges however short the steps A step stable in one node is stable in any chain Equilibrium The same The same

The prediction mu jumps at once when a new sample comes, when a node below learns and when the node itself learns; a node that holds r keeps its deviation in each case.

Sending mu instead of \(\mu + r\) is the fixed prediction assumption of predictive coding, and cuts the loop through the nodes above back to the node.

Given to Output Usually Sample, Activity, Prediction of pc.msg Messages The types of the data that flows (connections) Sample usually pc.Input Node Sends the x the host wrote as the activity. Holds nothing When built by hand pc.Layer Node Holds one module, moves r and lam, and learns the weights When built by hand pc.Output Node Holds the last module and the loss, sends the prediction, and learns the weights. No r or lam When built by hand pc.relax.Euler Settings The default relaxer, which moves r in time (relaxer) Left as default pc.clock.LearnClock Part Decides when to learn (LearnClock) Nodes of your own pc.functional Functions Formulas without state (vjp, loss_vjp, relax_) Nodes of your own pc.msg.activity_spec Function Makes the spec of an Activity Nodes of your own

Sends the gradient \(\partial\ell/\partial h_{\mathrm{in}}\) of the loss \(\ell = \sum_b \mathrm{mask}_b\,\ell_b\) as g_in 4 Sends an Activity Sends a Prediction 5 When to learn, optimizer.step_ As in Layer

docs.title: LearnClock
docs.text:
Host writes (time) Node new learns learns learns elapsed ≈ L time + L time + 2L time + 3L run's timer → L is a positive learn_interval

Each learning step is weighted by the elapsed (the time since it last learned) of the Tick, so the steps follow the gradient flow, and how far a node learns depends on time, not on how often it updates.

\[W \leftarrow W - \frac{\text{elapsed}}{\tau}\,\nabla \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \tau \dot W = -\nabla\]

LearnClock counts from the time time the host wrote the input, not the time the node received it, so the nodes on a path learn at about the same time, however deep they are (counted from receipt, deeper nodes would learn later, from a delta that has not yet answered the weights the nodes below have learned). How not to learn is in Choosing the optimizer.

docs.title: TimeConstants
docs.text:
Value The speed of With math.inf tau.h The relaxation of the deviation r Not allowed (finite and > 0) tau.lam How fast lam sums up r lam stays 0. r does not return to 0, and holds the credit instead tau.r How fast the deviation r decays No decay. Still stable, but delta takes more than one update to follow -g Why usually tau.r = tau.h, tau.lam = tau.h / 2 and a period of tau.h / 2?

With these, an update of one period moves delta = r + lam to -g exactly, without overshooting, and the node sends it back in that same update. A longer step overshoots, and the overshoot grows at every node it passes. The default period is period, and the longest dt one update counts is max_dt; both follow from the time constants.

TimeConstants holds the time constants of r and lam in seconds; the time constant of the weights belongs to the optimizer. How it relates to tau.h is in Choosing the time constants, and how long the credit takes to come back in The credit round trip.

docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["pc.optim.AdamW(...)<br/>setting, no state"] -->|"bind(params)"| B0["Layer 0: bound optimizer<br/>m, v, c_m, c_v"]
    S -->|"bind(params)"| B1["Layer 1: bound optimizer<br/>m, v, c_m, c_v"]
    S -->|"bind(params)"| B2["Output: bound optimizer<br/>m, v, c_m, c_v"]

An optimizer moves the weights as a flow in time, and each step moves it by the elapsed seconds the step covers, so how often a node learns does not change how fast its weights move per second.

1 0.632 0.393 0 0 0.05 0.1 0.15 0.2 total seconds of the steps (s) → c_m c_m = 1 − e^(−t/τ_m), τ_m = 0.1 s 0.05 s × 2 and 0.1 s × 1 both give 0.632 counting steps with β fixed, 0.1 s × 1 gives 0.393 The mass c_m used for bias correction (the share of the moment made of gradients so far) depends only on the total seconds of the steps. A correction that counts steps drifts when the length of the steps changes pc.optim (\(\beta = e^{-\Delta t/\tau}\), \(\Delta t\) the time between two learning steps) The matching torch optimizer Bias correction in torch When the steps match (constant \(\Delta t\)) AdamW torch.optim.AdamW Divides by \(1 - \beta^t\), \(t\) the number of steps From the first step SGD (given tau_m) torch.optim.SGD (momentum=β, dampening=β) None (the buffer starts from the first gradient) Once the mass is 1 (the difference decays as \(\beta^t\)). For a constant \(g\), from the first step RMSProp torch.optim.RMSprop (alpha=β) None (the mean square starts from 0) Once the mass is 1 (the difference decays as \(\beta^t\))

Why not torch.optim is in mujou.pc.optim.

docs.title: Relaxers
docs.text:
Optimizer Relaxer What it moves The weights \(\theta\), by elapsed seconds The deviation r, by dt seconds Along The gradient The force \(F\) on r (pc.relax) Base classes for one of your own Optimizer, BoundOptimizer Relaxer, BoundRelaxer Default None (required) pc.relax.Euler() Output Takes one Takes none (it has no r)

Neither r nor the force jumps when the prediction jumps, so reset_ is called only when the node first sees a sample whose reset is set.

docs.title: 🧠 PC-ALM
docs.text: mujou.pc splits a PyTorch model into nodes and learns it with PC-ALM (Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding, https://pub.sakana.ai/pc-alm/). How it works is in How mujou.pc Works and how to use it in 5. Learn with PC-ALM; this page covers how to choose the values.

The child names input, layer0, …, output of a pc.Chain are also the paths in run.state_dict().

docs.title: Building the nodes one by one
docs.text: pc.Chain runs every node on the same period. For a different period per node, or a shape other than a chain, build pc.Input, pc.Layer and pc.Output one by one and connect them. To show it samples with pc.show, inherit pc.Shown as well as mujou.Network, and expose the prev of the Input and the next of the Output as the network's prev and next.

The others follow from it 4 ms tau.r tau.h 4 ms tau.lam tau.h / 2 2 ms The period The default tau.period (tau.h / 2 with tau.r = tau.h) 2 ms max_dt The default tau.max_dt (1 period with the values above) 2 ms The showing time S periods, with S a few periods more than the round trip of the credit, 2 × hops periods 16 periods, 32 ms learn_interval Longer than half of the showing time, shorter than the showing time, and longer than 2 × hops × period (table below). MNIST uses 3/4 of the showing time 24 ms tau of the optimizer Much longer than tau.h (the weights learn from the settled delta). For values, see the conversion table pc.optim.SGD(tau=0.32) Host writes writes the next Node learns (24 ms) credit round trip ≤ 2 × 3 × 2 ms = 12 ms 0 12 ms S/2 = 16 ms S = 32 ms range for learn_interval run's timer → learn_interval Result Shorter than half of the showing time Learns twice or more per batch Longer than half of the showing time, but shorter than it Learns once per batch (the recommended range) As long as the showing time or longer The next batch is written first, and the node never learns Shorter than 2 × hops × period Not checked.
