docs.title: The round trip of the credit
docs.text: How the nodes run Time for the credit to go back one hop Round trip (the input to the Output, the credit back to the first Layer) ManualRun.step(dt) (every node once per step) 1 step Exactly 2 × hops steps mujou.run, every node with the same period At most 1 period About hops periods (at most 2 × hops periods) Different periods Up to about 1 period of the node it goes to Only a bound

docs.title: Choosing the optimizer
docs.text:
Optimizer One learning step of elapsed seconds pc.optim.SGD(tau=..., tau_m=None) p -= (elapsed / tau) * g. With tau_m, m_hat (momentum, the gradient averaged with the time constant tau_m) instead of g pc.optim.RMSProp(tau=..., tau_v=..., eps=1e-8) RMSProp with the learning rate elapsed / tau. The mean square v decays with the time constant tau_v pc.optim.AdamW(tau=..., tau_m=..., tau_v=..., ...) AdamW with the learning rate elapsed / tau. The moments m and v decay with the time constants tau_m and tau_v pc.optim.TimeScaled(optimizer, scale=...) Steps optimizer by elapsed * scale seconds (one stream)

Δt is the time between two learning steps: the showing time when the nodes learn once per batch.

Optimizer Behavior Converting from torch Measured with mujou.pc SGD Moves in proportion to the gradient tau = the showing time / the learning rate per batch MNIST SGD with momentum Averages the gradient over about the last tau_m seconds and keeps the learning rate: with a constant gradient, it moves as without momentum From torch.optim.SGD(lr, momentum=beta, dampening=beta), tau = Δt / lr and tau_m = -Δt / ln(beta). To match torch's default dampening=0, tau = (1 - beta) * Δt / lr Not measured yet RMSProp Divides the gradient by the root of its mean square, without momentum or weight decay. Moves each weight by up to about elapsed / tau per step From torch.optim.RMSprop(lr, alpha, eps), tau = Δt / lr and tau_v = -Δt / ln(alpha) Not measured yet AdamW Moves each weight by about elapsed / tau per step, whatever the size of its gradient From lr and betas of torch.optim.AdamW, tau = Δt / lr, tau_m = -Δt / ln(beta1) and tau_v = -Δt / ln(beta2). With a constant Δt, the steps are those of torch.optim.AdamW CIFAR-10

For a node that never learns, pass learn_interval=math.inf, not an infinite tau of the optimizer.

AvoidWrite instead 
optimizer = pc.optim.SGD(tau=math.inf)  # ValueError

# Give it to that pc.Layer or pc.Output. pc.Chain gives one learn_interval to every node
layer = pc.Layer(module, act_spec=spec, tau=tau, optimizer=optimizer, learn_interval=math.inf)

docs.title: Choosing the relaxer
docs.text: relaxer= of pc.Layer and pc.Chain is optional, and the default is pc.relax.Euler. pc.Output has no r, so it takes no relaxer. How relaxers work, and how to write your own, is in How mujou.pc Works.

docs.title: The batch
docs.text: batch x (784 inputs) y (one class) mask For () (default) (784,) () () One sample at a time, as from a sensor 64 (64, 784) (64,) (64,) 64 samples (8, 4) (8, 4, 784) (8, 4) (8, 4) 4 agents in each of 8 environments, for example. Learns as batch=32 64 (64, T, 784) (64,) (64,) 64 sequences of T steps. The time the module mixes is a dimension of the sample, not the batch

docs.title: One stream as a batch of consecutive samples
docs.text:
Batch (c = 4; the numbers are the indices of the samples in the stream) Row 0 Row 1 Row 2 Row 3 1st 0 1 2 3 2nd 4 5 6 7 3rd 8 9 10 11 Step Setting Why Difference from a run of one sample at a time 1 Show each batch for the time of one sample of the stream. This is the showing time Showing it c times as long as well would scale the time twice: the weights would learn c times too fast — 2 Write the time constants of optimizer in the stream's seconds, as for a run of one sample at a time TimeScaled divides them by c, so none is forgotten Compared with the sum of c steps of one sample, the step of one batch is the same to first order with pc.optim.SGD, and 1 to about √c times as large with RMSProp and AdamW (the mean gradient is less noisy) 3 Wrap the optimizer of every node that learns in the same pc.optim.TimeScaled(optimizer, scale=c) (the optimizer= of a pc.Chain) A node with another scale learns faster or slower than the rest The weights take one step over c times the time instead of c steps. A large c can lag behind, or learn too fast and become unstable 4 Choose tau.h, tau.r, tau.lam, the period and learn_interval from this showing time, as in Choosing the time constants They all stay in the run's seconds. TimeScaled changes only the time of the weights With reset False, each row continues from the sample c before it (the same row of the previous batch), not from the one just before

If the steps of RMSProp or AdamW are too large, lengthen tau. Good factors have not been measured yet.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Pitfall Symptom Fix The batch given to only the chain or the loss (batch is not read from the spec shapes) Given to neither, the credit of each sample is 1/64 (with 64 samples). Given to one only, an error The same batch to pc.Chain (or pc.Input) and to the loss A loss that averages over the batch (nn.MSELoss() and the like) pc.Output raises ValueError A loss that returns the loss of each sample, such as pc.loss.MSELoss(batch) Reading predictions from a Layer's next It does not hold the prediction of the network The next of pc.Output (net.next of a pc.Chain) Reading before the first sample arrives A prediction with mask all False Match time with the time write returned (as pc.show does) Heavy load Divergence, or a drop in accuracy. MNIST stops when y_hat is not finite; a run that diverges with finite predictions shows only as a falling accuracy Lower the time scale. Run on an otherwise idle machine (table below) No reset for shuffled samples The nodes near the input learn from the credit of unrelated samples reset True for samples that do not continue the one before (reset) AvoidWrite instead 
net = pc.Chain(*modules, x=TensorSpec((64, 784)), y=y_spec, loss=pc.loss.MSELoss(), ...)  # credit 1/64
out = pc.Output(module, act_spec=spec, loss=nn.MSELoss(), ...)  # ValueError

net = pc.Chain(*modules, x=TensorSpec((64, 784)), y=y_spec, batch=64, loss=pc.loss.MSELoss(64), ...)
out = pc.Output(module, act_spec=spec, loss=pc.loss.MSELoss(64), ...)

If a node runs late, its neighbors keep learning from its old messages. Two causes are known. max_dt does not prevent this: it caps the time one update counts, and the time beyond it is dropped from the relaxation and from the weight update alike.

Cause of the load Observed Fix A time scale that is too fast The examples speed up the run's timer with --time-scale. Too fast, and the slowest node takes longer than its period to compute. In CIFAR-10 with a node for each residual block, at a period of 2 ms of real time, the updates came 1.1 to 1.3 periods apart on average with stalls of up to 100 periods, and the accuracy fell by about 20 points Run one epoch with --watch (MNIST) and take the highest time scale that gives no warning and does not diverge Other processes on the cores A node that waits for a core lets its neighbors run ahead. On 32 cores at time scale 1, one epoch ran through beside 26 busy loops and diverged beside 32; at 0.5 it ran through beside 32 Run on an otherwise idle machine, or lower the time scale

docs.title: Nodes of your own
docs.text:
Write a node that pc.Layer cannot express (one with several inputs, say) by combining the formulas of pc.functional with pc.clock.LearnClock, an optimizer and a relaxer. Keep the stages of one update as in One update of a Layer, bind the optimizer and the relaxer in each node, and do not share a bound one between nodes.

flowchart LR
    H1["Host"] -->|"Sample"| I["inp<br/>pc.Input"]
    I -->|"Activity"| A["a<br/>pc.Layer"]
    I -->|"Activity"| B["b<br/>pc.Layer"]
    A -->|"Activity → port a"| M["merge<br/>Merge"]
    B -->|"Activity → port b"| M
    M -->|"Activity"| O["out<br/>pc.Output"]
    O -->|"Prediction"| H2["Host"]
    M -.->|"sends back g_a (the part for h_a)"| A
    M -.->|"sends back g_b (the part for h_b)"| B
class Merge(Node):
    """``mu = module(cat(h_a, h_b))``: a node of PC-ALM with two inputs."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        module: nn.Module,
        a: DictSpec[pc.msg.Activity],
        b: DictSpec[pc.msg.Activity],
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=TAU.period)
        self.module = module
        self.optimizer = OPTIMIZER.bind(self.module.parameters())
        self.clock = pc.clock.LearnClock.of(
            TAU, period=self.period, learn_interval=None
        )
        h_a, h_b = a.field("h", TensorSpec), b.field("h", TensorSpec)
        self.sizes = [h_a.shape[-1], h_b.shape[-1]]
        h = TensorSpec((B, module(torch.zeros(B, sum(self.sizes))).shape[-1]))
        self.r, self.lam = h.zeros(), h.zeros()  # r = h - mu
        self.act_spec = pc.msg.activity_spec(h, a.field("y", TensorSpec), B)
        self.a = Port(send=h_a, recv=a)  # sends back g_in of h_a
        self.b = Port(send=h_b, recv=b)
        self.next = MultiPort(send=self.act_spec, recv=h)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        a, b = self.a.recv(), self.b.recv()
        t = self.clock.tick(dt, a["time"], self.timer.now())
        if t.new:  # the samples that start anew drop the credit of the ones before
            new = a["reset"].unsqueeze(-1)
            self.r.masked_fill_(new, 0.0)
            self.lam.masked_fill_(new, 0.0)
        labeled = a["mask"].unsqueeze(-1)  # a sample without a target sends no credit
        g = sum(self.next.recv().values(), torch.zeros_like(self.r))
        pc.functional.relax_(self.r, self.lam, g, t.dt, TAU)
        delta = torch.where(labeled, self.r + self.lam, 0)
        params = list(self.module.parameters())
        mu, g_in, g_theta = pc.functional.vjp(
            self.module, torch.cat([a["h"], b["h"]], dim=-1), lambda _: delta, params
        )
        g_a, g_b = g_in.split(self.sizes, dim=-1)
        self.a.send(g_a)
        self.b.send(g_b)
        # The prediction goes on, with the y, mask, reset and time of a.
        self.next.send({**a, "h": mu})
        if a["mask"].any():  # nothing to learn from samples without a target
            self.optimizer.step_([g_p / B for g_p in g_theta], t.elapsed)
Differs from pc.Layer in Merge (examples/pc_merge.py) Ports One for each input (a and b) g_in Split by the widths of h_a and h_b into g_a and g_b, each sent back from its own port

docs.title: The kinds of ports
docs.text:
Kind Peers recv() returns Port At most one if it receives; any number if it only sends The value MultiPort Any number, of one role A dict[Channel, value], in connect order

Inputs of different roles, such as an input and its teacher signal, or a prediction and an error, go to separate Ports, each named after its role. A MultiPort is for peers of one role that the node combines the same way.

AvoidWrite instead 
class Bad(Node):
    prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)  # class attribute: the class statement raises TypeError

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.inputs = [Port(recv=VECTOR), Port(recv=VECTOR)]  # list: the run raises TypeError

class Good(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()  # declare ports after this
        self.a = Port(recv=VECTOR)  # one attribute per port
        self.b = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.many = MultiPort(recv=VECTOR)  # any number of peers of one role

docs.title: Specs
docs.text:
Spec Used for Initial value TensorSpec One tensor, such as an activity or an error Zeros IntSpec, FloatSpec, BoolSpec, TimestampSpec A count, a flag, a time 0, 0.0, False, Timestamp(ns=0) DictSpec Values to deliver together, such as an input and its target (a TypedDict) The initial value per key

A count, a flag or a time travels as a Python scalar with a scalar spec, not wrapped in a tensor, so the receiver uses it without int(...).

docs.title: Values that belong together: DictSpec
docs.text:
Values on two ports arrive separately, so a reader may pair a new value on one with an old value on the other. Put values that belong together, such as an input and its target, in one DictSpec, and the whole dict arrives at once.

class Sample(TypedDict):
    x: torch.Tensor
    y: torch.Tensor


SAMPLE = DictSpec(Sample, x=TensorSpec((32, 4)), y=TensorSpec((32, 2)))

self.next = Port(send=SAMPLE)  # in the sender: self.next.send({"x": x, "y": y})
self.prev = Port(recv=SAMPLE)  # in the receiver: sample = self.prev.recv(); sample["x"]

docs.title: Type annotations
docs.text:
Type checkers infer the type of a port from its specs. Annotate only when you need to (for an argument of a helper, say), as Port[S, R] or MultiPort[S, R] (sends S, receives R); a direction left out is Never, so a type checker rejects send on a port that sends nothing. Annotate a function that takes any spec with MessageSpec.

def mean_of(port: MultiPort[Never, torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
    return torch.stack(list(port.recv().values())).mean(0)

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text: connect joins ports only: nodes and networks have no connect of their own. A node may have many inputs and outputs, and naming both ports makes the path readable. Cycles (the nodes of mujou.pc make them with two-way ports) and two ports of the same node are allowed. A port connected to one outside the tree being run makes mujou.run raise ValueError.

docs.title: Fan-out and merging
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IN(["Input x"]) --> SH["shift<br/>x + 1"]
    SH -->|"same value to both"| D["double<br/>2x"]
    SH --> SQ["square<br/>x²"]
    D --> SUM["sum (MultiPort)<br/>adds the latest value of each channel"]
    SQ --> SUM
    SUM --> OUT(["Output y = 2(x + 1) + (x + 1)²"])
class Apply(Node):
    """Sends ``fn(x)``."""

    def __init__(self, fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fn = fn
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)  # only sends: any number of peers

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.fn(self.prev.recv()))


class Sum(Node):
    """Sends the sum of the latest messages of all its peers."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = MultiPort(recv=VECTOR)  # merges any number of peers
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        received = self.prev.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor], in connect order
        self.next.send(torch.stack(list(received.values())).sum(dim=0))


class Diamond(mujou.Network):
    """``shift -> (double, square) -> sum``: y = 2 (x + 1) + (x + 1)^2."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.shift = Apply(lambda x: x + 1)
        self.double = Apply(lambda x: 2 * x)
        self.square = Apply(lambda x: x**2)
        self.sum = Sum()
        self.shift.next.connect(self.double.prev)  # one port, two peers
        self.shift.next.connect(self.square.prev)
        self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev)  # two peers, one MultiPort
        self.square.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.shift.prev, self.sum.next

The receiving node decides how to combine the values: sum them, average them, weight each peer.

docs.title: Treating peers differently
docs.text:
To treat peers differently, keep the Channel that connect returned as an attribute of the receiving node, and use it as a key into the dict of recv().

# the network
self.sum.from_double = self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev)

# the receiving node (sum)
x = self.prev.recv()[self.from_double]

docs.title: Sending to one channel
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IN(["Input x"]) --> SP["split (MultiPort)"]
    SP -->|"send_to(plus, x)"| P["pos<br/>relu"]
    SP -->|"send_to(minus, -x)"| N["neg<br/>relu"]
    P --> SUM["sum"]
    N --> SUM
    SUM --> OUT(["Output y = relu(x) + relu(-x)<br/>(absolute value of x)"])
class Split(Node):
    """Sends ``x`` on the channel ``plus`` and ``-x`` on the channel ``minus``."""

    # Channels of self.next, set by the network to the ones connect returned.
    plus: Channel
    minus: Channel

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = MultiPort(send=VECTOR)  # sends to each peer on its own

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()
        self.next.send_to(self.plus, x)
        self.next.send_to(self.minus, -x)


class Magnitude(mujou.Network):
    """``split -> (relu, relu) -> sum``: y = relu(x) + relu(-x) = |x|."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.split = Split()
        self.pos, self.neg = Apply(torch.relu), Apply(torch.relu)
        self.sum = Sum()
        # Hand split the channels it sends on: the order of connect does not matter.
        self.split.plus = self.split.next.connect(self.pos.prev)
        self.split.minus = self.split.next.connect(self.neg.prev)
        self.pos.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.neg.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.split.prev, self.sum.next

The network hands send_to its channels by assigning what connect returned to attributes of the node. An attribute that holds a Channel is not part of the state.

AvoidWrite instead 
# swapping the connect calls silently swaps plus and minus
self.split.plus, self.split.minus = self.split.next.channels

self.split.plus = self.split.next.connect(self.pos.prev)
self.split.minus = self.split.next.connect(self.neg.prev)

docs.title: A new value, or the same one again
docs.text:
value, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
if t is not None and t != self.last_t:  # a new value arrived since the last read
    self.last_t = t

Until the sender first sends, recv_with_time returns the initial value with the time None. The initial values of ports the host writes are in Initial values.

docs.title: Two ways to run
docs.text:
mujou.run mujou.run_manually For Deploying to the real world (sensors, robots) Simulating an environment, training faster than real time, testing Time Real time (global_timer by default); sleeps to follow it Virtual time: a VirtualTimer that only step moves; no sleeping, as fast as the machine period Each node updates every period on average Not used; once in each step that updates the node Results Vary from run to run The same, bit for bit, every time Returns Run ManualRun, a Run with step Why not mujou.run with a large time scale?

A Timer with time_scale=10 runs ten times faster, but the nodes still update when the machine lets them: dt varies, and so do the results. It also cannot go faster than the time scale, however fast the machine is. A ManualRun moves the time only when the last step is done.

docs.title: A simulation loop
docs.text:
This loop feeds a sine wave to the LeakyChain of Write a Node for 2 s of virtual time, in steps of 1 ms. One pass writes the input of the next step with run.write, then calls run.step(H); reads happen between steps (here, after the last one).

def simulate(seconds: float, workers: int | None = None) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Feed a sine of 1 Hz to a new chain for ``seconds`` of virtual time and
    return its last output."""
    net = LeakyChain(TAU)
    with mujou.run_manually(net, workers=workers) as run:
        for i in range(round(seconds / H)):
            # Write between steps: the input for the step about to run.
            u = math.sin(2 * math.pi * i * H)
            run.write({net.prev: torch.tensor(u, dtype=SCALAR.dtype)})
            run.step(H)  # 1 ms later, then every node once, in parallel
        return run.read(net.next)


start = time.perf_counter()
y = simulate(2.0)
print(f"2 s simulated in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f} s of real time")
# The same result, bit for bit, with any number of workers.
assert torch.equal(y, simulate(2.0, workers=1))

docs.title: The two kinds of step
docs.text:
Use step(dt) unless the order matters to you, as when you compare a node with an algorithm that updates a, then b. Both move the timer dt forward first, then update; the full rules are in ManualRun.step.

run.step(h) (Jacobi)run.step(h, net.a, net.b) (Gauss-Seidel) 
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant R as ManualRun
    participant A as net.a
    participant B as net.b
    H->>R: run.step(h)
    R->>R: moves the virtual timer h forward
    par on the workers, in parallel
        R->>A: on_update(h)
    and
        R->>B: on_update(h), reading a's value from the start of the step
    end
    Note over A,B: what a and b sent becomes visible now
    R-->>H: returns
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant R as ManualRun
    participant A as net.a
    participant B as net.b
    H->>R: run.step(h, net.a, net.b)
    R->>R: moves the virtual timer h forward
    R->>A: on_update(h)
    A-->>B: send (visible at once)
    R->>B: on_update(h), reading a's new value
    R-->>H: returns

docs.title: Matching an order
docs.text:
Compare three ways to step the chain u → a → b. Giving every node is not always the same as step(dt).

def output_after(steps: int, order: str) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Step a new chain ``steps`` times with a constant input of 1 and return its
    output. ``order`` is "at once", "a, b" or "b, a"."""
    net = LeakyChain(TAU)
    nodes = {"at once": (), "a, b": (net.a, net.b), "b, a": (net.b, net.a)}[order]
    with mujou.run_manually(net, inputs={net.prev: ONE}) as run:
        for _ in range(steps):
            run.step(H, *nodes)
        return run.read(net.next)


at_once = output_after(3, "at once")  # b reads the a of the start of each step
assert torch.equal(at_once, output_after(3, "b, a"))  # b, then a: the same
assert not torch.equal(at_once, output_after(3, "a, b"))  # b reads the new a
print(f"after 3 steps: b = {at_once.item():.6f} (at once and b, a)")
print(f"after 3 steps: b = {output_after(3, 'a, b').item():.6f} (a, b)")
Way to step The a that b reads Result step(h) The a of the start of the step Reference step(h, net.b, net.a) The old a (b updates first) The same as step(h) step(h, net.a, net.b) The a sent in this step Different

docs.title: dt across steps
docs.text: start h 2h 3h net.a dt = h dt = h dt = h net.b dt = 3h (the time of the two steps it missed adds up) Steps 1 and 2 are step(h, net.a), step 3 is step(h). Each vertical line is an update

docs.title: Keeping it deterministic
docs.text:
Keep these rules, and a ManualRun gives the same result, bit for bit, every time, whatever the number of workers and whichever thread runs which node (to keep torch's threads from competing for the cores with many workers, see Settings of the whole process).

Rule Why Draw random numbers from self.generator, with a seed The default generator is shared by every node, in an order that varies (Seeds) Move the time only with step; do not call run.timer.advance The nodes would get a dt you did not plan Call write between steps A write during a step reaches some nodes in that step and others in the next Do not share Python objects between nodes Nodes that append to one list, say, do it in a different order each time On the thread that steps, do not call wait_for, subscribe or run.timer.sleep; use read Nothing is sent and no time passes until the next step, so they wait until their timeout (forever without one) To keep several runs in step, pass one VirtualTimer to each They share one time axis, and a step of one run moves the time of the others too 
timer = mujou.time.VirtualTimer()  # several runs share one time axis
with (
    mujou.run_manually(a, timer=timer) as run_a,
    mujou.run_manually(b, timer=timer) as run_b,
):
    run_a.step(0.001)  # run_b's timer moves 1 ms too

docs.title: Step boundaries are only for simulation
docs.text:
An update rule must not rely on step boundaries. A network that works only under run.step(dt) fails when it is deployed with mujou.run (rules a node keeps).

Between two steps of a ManualRun mujou.run Updates of every node Finished Each node at its own times, out of step Time Stands still. The boundary is part of no node; it happens in between Keeps moving A moment when all nodes align Yes No What a node reads Only its own state and its neighbors' latest values; it does not know it is in a ManualRun The same

docs.title: Saving, resuming and errors
docs.text: Take the state between steps with run.state_dict() and pass it to new instances with mujou.run_manually(..., state=tree): the steps after it give the same result as a run that did not stop (Test a Node). When a node raises, step raises NetworkError (Errors and Shutdown; how to write it in pytest is in Test a Node).

docs.title: 🧵 Threads and Devices
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["mujou.run"] --> P["Pool of workers<br/>(workers threads)"]
    R --> D["Dedicated threads<br/>(one per node)"]
    P -->|"share the nodes"| N1["Node"]
    P --> N2["Node"]
    P --> N3["Node"]
    D --> N4["Node with<br/>dedicated_thread=True"]

docs.title: The workers
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Q["Scheduled updates (earliest due first)"]
        direction TB
        U1["update of node C"] ~~~ U2["update of node A"] ~~~ U3["update of node B"]
    end
    Q -->|"after one hook, take the next"| W1["Worker 1"]
    Q --> W2["Worker 2"]

A run does not start a thread per node, so with many nodes the threads stay few, and the OS does not spend its time switching between them. The number of workers and its default are under workers of mujou.run.

Why is the default halved while the GIL is enabled?

While the GIL is enabled (on a build of Python with it, or on the free-threaded build with PYTHON_GIL=1), one thread runs Python code at a time, so the nodes run in parallel only inside torch operations. More workers than half the CPUs mostly contend for the GIL, which is why the default is half. For nodes that spend most of their time in Python, even fewer are about as fast.

docs.title: A thread of its own
docs.text:
Pass dedicated_thread=True to a node whose hooks block, waiting for a device, a socket or a lock, or that relies on per-thread state set once in on_start.

class Camera(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=1 / 30, dedicated_thread=True)

docs.title: Per-thread settings
docs.text:
Setting On the workers How to write it threading.local, threading.current_thread(), threading.get_ident() May differ from hook to hook For a setting made once, a dedicated thread Per-thread settings of torch (torch.autocast, gradient recording, and so on) Left behind, they leak into the next node on the same worker Keep them inside a with in the hook contextvars Carry over. Each node runs its hooks in a contextvars.Context of its own, which starts empty (it does not inherit the host's) Use as is The current CUDA device and stream Mujou sets them before each hook of a CUDA node. This is the only thing Mujou itself sets — AvoidWrite instead 
@override
def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
    super().on_update(dt)
    torch.set_grad_enabled(False)  # left behind, it leaks into the next node on the worker
    ...

@override
def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
    super().on_update(dt)
    with torch.no_grad():  # set back before the hook returns
        ...

docs.title: Seeds and random numbers
docs.text:
seed reproduces only the node's own generator, self.generator, so initialize nn.Linear and the like again from it (the default initialization uses the generator every node shares).

AvoidWrite instead 
super().__init__(seed=0)
torch.manual_seed(0)  # changes the random numbers of the other nodes too
self.model = nn.Linear(4, 2)  # initialized from the generator every node shares

super().__init__(seed=0)
self.model = nn.Linear(4, 2)
nn.init.normal_(self.model.weight, std=0.1, generator=self.generator)
nn.init.zeros_(self.model.bias)

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: Received messages arrive on the node's device, so allocate tensors with device=self.device. A state tree taken from CUDA nodes restores only into CUDA nodes (on another machine with a GPU too; why is in Node.load_state_dict).

docs.title: What Mujou does for a CUDA node
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Worker
    participant N as CUDA node
    participant S as Node's own stream
    W->>N: make the device and stream current
    W->>N: on_update(dt)
    N->>S: queue operations
    W->>S: wait for the queued work
    Note over W: then on to the next work
    Note over W,S: around taking the state, a thread of Mujou's own waits, not a worker

Each CUDA node has a stream of its own, and Mujou switches to it and waits for it, so the node writes no synchronization.

docs.title: How a message travels
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["CUDA node<br/>sends a tensor on its device"] -->|"if a CUDA node reads the port:<br/>copied on the node's stream,<br/>kept on the device"| P(("port"))
    P -->|"device to device,<br/>no host memory in between<br/>(without peer access the driver may stage it)"| B["CUDA node"]
    P -->|"a CPU copy when read"| C["CPU node<br/>host"]

The full rules are in Port.send, and the host's writes in Run.write. A node that reads messages from a CUDA node on another device (a node on the CPU, or on another GPU) copies them on a stream of its own on that device, which Mujou makes current in each of its hooks too. A node on the CPU that reads no CUDA node does not touch CUDA, nor does it use the stream of a CUDA node left on the worker.

docs.title: Synchronization and streams
docs.text:
AvoidWrite instead 
torch.cuda.synchronize()  # waits for the whole device, the other nodes' work included

torch.cuda.current_stream().record_event().synchronize()  # only your own stream

Streams come from a pool of 32 per device, counting the nodes' streams and the copy streams of the nodes that read another device. Past 32, some nodes share a stream: the results stay correct, but a reader that shares the writer's stream also waits for what the writer queued after it sent, which may slow it down (a node on the CPU waits for it on the host).

Create CUDA tensors and modules in on_start

Tensors and modules made on CUDA in __init__ work, since mujou.run synchronizes the host's stream before it starts the nodes. Still, create them in on_start or later. PyTorch's caching allocator ties memory to the stream current when it was allocated, so memory allocated in __init__ stays tied to the host's stream; when the node drops such a tensor, the memory may be reused by the host before the node's work on it has finished. A restore loads the state after on_start, so state made there is restored too.

AvoidWrite instead 
def __init__(self) -> None:
    super().__init__(device="cuda:0")
    self.w = torch.zeros(256, 256, device=self.device)  # tied to the host's stream

@override
def on_start(self) -> None:
    super().on_start()
    self.w = torch.zeros(256, 256, device=self.device)  # allocated on the node's stream

docs.title: Settings of the whole process
docs.text:
Do not change settings the whole process shares in a node. The host sets them once, before mujou.run.

Kind Settings and operations Random numbers torch.manual_seed and the default random generator Behavior of torch torch.set_num_threads, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms, the flags of torch.backends.* Operations on a whole device torch.cuda.synchronize(), torch.cuda.empty_cache(), and so on 
# The nodes compute on the run's worker threads, and torch adds threads of its
# own for each: keep those few (a setting of the whole process, made by the host).
torch.set_num_threads(1)

Rule of thumb for the number of threads

(workers + nodes with dedicated_thread=True) × n ≤ physical cores

n is the value of torch.set_num_threads(n). With many nodes on small matrices, n = 1 is enough.

docs.title: ⏱️ Time
docs.text: Each run has one time axis: every node's dt, every message's time and every pause are on the run's timer (why nodes update by dt is in Time in How Mujou Works).

docs.title: The timers
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q{"How is it run?"}
    Q -- "mujou.run(net)" --> G["global_timer<br/>shared with other runs"]
    Q -- "mujou.run(net, timer=Timer())" --> O["The Timer passed<br/>for that run only"]
    Q -- "mujou.run(net, state=tree)" --> R["A new Timer<br/>starting at the tree's time"]
    Q -- "mujou.run_manually(net)" --> V["VirtualTimer<br/>moves only when advanced"]

The timer types (Timer, VirtualTimer, ReadOnlyTimer, Timestamp, global_timer) are in mujou.time.

docs.title: What the host and a node can do
docs.text:
Operation Host (run.timer) Node (self.timer) now(), time_scale() Yes Yes is_paused() Yes No such method sleep, pause, resume, set_time_scale, VirtualTimer.advance Yes No such method; in a hook, RuntimeError AvoidWrite instead 
def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
    super().on_update(dt)
    global_timer.sleep(0.1)  # RuntimeError in a hook

def __init__(self) -> None:
    super().__init__(period=0.1)  # updates every 0.1 s on average

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Unit Used by Seconds of the run's timer dt, period, Timer.sleep, VirtualTimer.advance, pc.show(seconds=), the time constants of mujou.pc Real seconds Every timeout Why is a timeout in real time?

So that a stuck run is given up on, whatever its time scale and pauses.

docs.title: Timestamp
docs.text:
A Timestamp does not record which timer it is on, so compare only times of one timer (those of one run and its run.timer.now(), say).

# A Timestamp: float(t) is seconds, .ns the exact nanoseconds; the difference of
# two is the seconds between them, a float (negative if the first is earlier).
t0, t1 = Timestamp(ns=1_500_000_000), Timestamp(ns=2_000_000_000)
assert float(t0) == 1.5 and t0.ns == 1_500_000_000
assert t1 - t0 == 0.5 and t0 - t1 == -0.5

t_in = run.write({net.prev: x})
run.timer.sleep(0.1)
y, t_out = run.read_with_time(net.next)
if t_out is not None and t_out >= t_in:  # y was sent after x was written
    print(t_out - t_in)  # seconds from the write until y was sent

docs.title: A timer of a run's own and its scale
docs.text:
Scaling or pausing the Timer passed to mujou.run does not affect other runs (whether to split runs or join them into one is in Groups).

# A run on a timer of its own, ten times faster than the real time. Pausing this
# timer (or taking this run's state) stops only this run, not the global timer.
timer = Timer(time_scale=10.0)  # starts at 0
clock = Clock()
start_real, start_global = time.perf_counter(), global_timer.now()
with mujou.run(clock, timer=timer) as run:
    run.timer.sleep(2.0)  # 2 s of the run's time: about 0.2 s of real time
    # When the clock updates depends on how the threads get scheduled: wait until
    # it has sent a time from 2 s on. The timeout is in real seconds.
    seen, t = run.wait_for(clock.next, lambda now: now.item() >= 2.0, timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None  # None only for the zeros before the first send
elapsed_real = time.perf_counter() - start_real
elapsed_global = global_timer.now() - start_global
print(
    f"run's time {float(t):.2f} s, real {elapsed_real:.2f} s, "
    f"global {elapsed_global:.2f} s"
)
# Compare times of the same timer only: a Timestamp does not say which it is on.
assert seen.item() <= float(t)

The global_timer can be scaled too, which changes every run on it.

# The global timer can be scaled too; it then applies to every run on it.
global_timer.set_time_scale(5.0)
start_real = time.perf_counter()
global_timer.sleep(0.5)  # 0.5 s of the global time: about 0.1 s of real time
print(f"slept 0.5 s of global time in {time.perf_counter() - start_real:.2f} s real")
global_timer.set_time_scale(1.0)

docs.title: Pausing the time
docs.text:
pause() resume() Time stops no updates, sleep does not return Node the next dt counts only the time before and after the pause real time →

From Timer.pause until resume, every run on that timer stops (global_timer.pause() stops every run on the global timer). Your pause and the pause for taking the state (Save and Resume) are separate switches.

A pause is for taking the state and for observing

Do not make it part of how a network learns.

docs.title: Taking the states of several runs at one time
docs.text:
# Two runs on the global timer, such as two agents that should be saved together.
# Taken one after the other, the second state would be of a later time; pausing
# the timer they share stops both at one time T.
a, b = Clock(), Clock()
with mujou.run(a) as run_a, mujou.run(b) as run_b:
    global_timer.sleep(0.1)
    global_timer.pause()  # the global time stops at one time T
    try:
        tree_a = run_a.state_dict()  # still works while paused
        tree_b = run_b.state_dict()
    finally:
        global_timer.resume()  # the time goes on from T
t_ns = tree_a["timer"]["time_ns"]
assert tree_b["timer"]["time_ns"] == t_ns  # both are of T
data = pickle.dumps({"a": tree_a, "b": tree_b})  # save them together
AvoidWrite instead 
global_timer.pause()
tree_a = run_a.state_dict()
tree_b = run_b.state_dict()
global_timer.resume()  # an exception in between leaves the time stopped

global_timer.pause()
try:
    tree_a = run_a.state_dict()
    tree_b = run_b.state_dict()
finally:
    global_timer.resume()  # resumes even on an exception

docs.title: The timer of a resumed run
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    G["a and b on global_timer<br/>states taken at time T"] --> TA["tree_a (time T)"]
    G --> TB2["tree_b (time T)"]
    TA -->|"mujou.run(a2, state=tree_a)"| RA["A new Timer<br/>moving on from T"]
    TB2 -->|"mujou.run(b2, state=tree_b)"| RB["Another new Timer<br/>moving on from T"]
    RA -.-|"drift apart; pausing one does not pause the other"| RB
# A run restored from one of them goes on from T on a timer of its own: the
# global timer does not go back.
saved = pickle.loads(data)
restored = Clock()
with mujou.run(restored, state=saved["a"]) as run:
    assert run.timer is not global_timer
    now, _ = run.wait_for(
        restored.next, lambda now: now.item() > t_ns / 1e9, timeout=5.0
    )
# After the run, its nodes' attributes are the host's to read.
at_save = saved["a"]["nodes"][""]["state"]["elapsed"].item()
print(
    f"run a went on from t = {t_ns / 1e9:.3f} s to {now.item():.3f} s; "
    f"its dt summed to {at_save:.3f} s at the save, {restored.elapsed.item():.3f} s now"
)

Runs that must stay on one time axis after a resume run as one run in a Group from the start (mujou.run(Group(a=a, b=b)); the tree of one run resumes onto one timer).

docs.title: 🧮 Update Rules
docs.text: How to choose an update rule is in How Mujou Works. This page shows a rule of your own that learns across nodes, with feedback alignment as the example.

docs.title: Feedback alignment
docs.text:
examples/feedback_alignment.py learns \(\hat y = W_2 \tanh(W_1 x)\) with two nodes, hidden and output. hidden does not know W2, and learns anyway with a fixed random matrix \(B\) (Lillicrap et al., 2016).

flowchart LR
    Host["Host"] -->|"sample x, y"| H["hidden<br/>h = tanh(W1 x)"]
    H -->|"activity h, target y, time"| O["output<br/>ŷ = W2 h"]
    O -->|"error e = ŷ − y, time"| H
    O -->|"loss"| Loss["read by the host"]
BP Feedback alignment Credit hidden uses \(W_2^\top e\) \(B e\) (\(B\) is a fixed random matrix of hidden) hidden must know W2 Yes No Why it learns It is the gradient \(W_2\) comes to align with \(B^\top\) 
uv run python examples/feedback_alignment.py

class Hidden(Node):
    """h = tanh(W1 x); learns W1 from the error that comes back through ``B``."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=PERIOD, seed=1)
        g = self.generator
        self.w1 = torch.randn(N_HIDDEN, N_IN, generator=g) / N_IN**0.5
        self.b = torch.randn(N_OUT, N_HIDDEN, generator=g) / N_OUT**0.5  # fixed
        self.optimizer = OPTIMIZER.bind([self.w1])
        self.clock = pc.clock.LearnClock(
            period=PERIOD, learn_interval=LEARN, max_dt=2 * PERIOD
        )
        self.prev = Port(recv=SAMPLE)  # the host writes it
        self.next = Port(send=ACTIVITY, recv=ERROR)  # two-way

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        sample, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
        if t is None:  # nothing written yet
            return
        x = sample["x"]
        h = torch.tanh(x @ self.w1.T)
        self.next.send({"h": h, "y": sample["y"], "time": t})  # relays y
        error = self.next.recv()
        tick = self.clock.tick(dt, t, self.timer.now())
        if tick.learn and error["time"] == t:  # the error of this sample
            delta = (error["e"] @ self.b) * (1 - h**2)  # B e, not W2^T e
            self.optimizer.step_([(delta.T @ x) / BATCH], tick.elapsed)

class Output(Node):
    """y_hat = W2 h; sends the error back, and the loss on each new sample."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=PERIOD, seed=2)
        self.w2 = torch.randn(N_OUT, N_HIDDEN, generator=self.generator) / N_HIDDEN
        self.optimizer = OPTIMIZER.bind([self.w2])
        self.clock = pc.clock.LearnClock(
            period=PERIOD, learn_interval=LEARN, max_dt=2 * PERIOD
        )
        self.prev = Port(send=ERROR, recv=ACTIVITY)  # two-way
        self.loss = Port(send=TensorSpec(()))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        act, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
        if t is None:  # hidden has not sent yet
            return
        h = act["h"]
        e = h @ self.w2.T - act["y"]  # the prediction against its own target
        self.prev.send({"e": e, "time": act["time"]})
        tick = self.clock.tick(dt, act["time"], self.timer.now())
        if tick.new:  # the first update with this sample, before learning from it
            self.loss.send(0.5 * e.pow(2).sum(dim=1).mean())
        if tick.learn:
            self.optimizer.step_([(e.T @ h) / BATCH], tick.elapsed)
Condition Printed loss of output (on each batch, before learning from it) Both nodes learn Falls from about 1.5 to about 0.02 in 6 s hidden frozen Stays above 0.15

docs.title: Two-way ports
docs.text:
This example carries the activity and the error on one connection (hidden.next and output.prev). Connections may form cycles, so the error could as well come back on ports of its own.

Port send recv hidden.next ACTIVITY ERROR output.prev ERROR ACTIVITY

docs.title: Relaying the target
docs.text:
Avoid: the target on a port of its ownWrite instead: one message 
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as hidden
    participant O as output
    H->>O: activity h (sample 2)
    Note over O: the target port still holds y of sample 1
    O->>O: compares the prediction for sample 2 with y of sample 1
    H->>O: target y (sample 2)
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as hidden
    participant O as output
    H->>O: h, y, time (sample 2)
    O->>O: compares the prediction with its own target
    O->>H: e, time
    H->>H: learns only from the error whose time is that of the input it holds

The nodes of mujou.pc also carry y, mask and time in the same message as the activity, a pc.msg.Activity.

recv() returns the latest value whether or not it is new, so a node that learns once from each sample tells a new one by its time (A new value, or the same one again).

docs.title: pc.clock.LearnClock
docs.text:
tick = self.clock.tick(dt, t, self.timer.now())  # dt, the time the input was written, the time now
if tick.learn:
    self.optimizer.step_([grad], tick.elapsed)  # weighted by the time since it last learned

LearnClock, which decides when to learn, is a part of mujou.pc, but any rule can use it. Weighing each step with elapsed makes how far a node learns depend on time, not on how often it updates (How mujou.pc Works).

docs.title: Write the page
docs.text:
class Plant(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.left = Filter()  # a network in a network
        self.right = Filter()
        self.monitor = Monitor()
        self.left.next.connect(self.monitor.prev)
        self.right.next.connect(self.monitor.prev)


net = Plant()
Path("graph.html").write_text(mujou.viz.to_html(net), "utf-8")  # open it in a browser

to_html reads the network tree as mujou.run does, but calls no hooks, starts no threads and runs nothing. So it shows the nodes by the same paths as a run (Networks and paths).

The page is one HTML file with nothing to download, so it opens offline too, and you can send it to someone as it is.

docs.title: 🚀 1. Run a Network
docs.text:
This page runs examples/quickstart.py, the smallest program, two nodes that compute \(y = 2x + 1\), and shows how to write a node, a network and a run.

flowchart LR
    H1["Host"] -->|"writes x to net.prev"| S["scale<br/>×2"]
    S --> F["shift<br/>+1"]
    F -->|"reads y from net.next"| H2["Host"]

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
examples/quickstart.py
"""The smallest program: two nodes in a network, running in the background.

The host writes an input, waits until the output arrives, and stops.
"""

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import Network, Node, Port, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((3,))  # every message here is a float32 vector of 3


class Affine(Node):
    """Sends ``a * x + b``, where ``x`` is the latest input."""

    def __init__(self, a: float, b: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = a, b  # settings, not state
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous node
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next node

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.a * self.prev.recv() + self.b)  # recv() never waits


class Pipeline(Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Affine(2.0, 0.0)
        self.shift = Affine(1.0, 1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.scale.prev, self.shift.next  # exposed as its own


net = Pipeline()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on the run's worker threads until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None  # None only for the zeros before the first send

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
From a source checkoutInstalled from PyPI

From the root of the repository:

uv run python examples/quickstart.py

Copy examples/quickstart.py to your machine, then:

python quickstart.py

y = tensor([3., 5., 7.]) at t = 0.017 s

t is the time, in seconds of the run's timer, at which shift sent y. It changes every run.

docs.title: The node
docs.text:
Affine inherits from Node and creates its ports as attributes in __init__. By convention the port that receives from the previous node is prev and the one that sends to the next is next; a and b are settings from the arguments, not state.

One step of work goes in on_update(dt), which mujou calls again and again: it reads with recv and sends with send.

docs.text: What Pipeline (Network) does Code Holds nodes as attributes self.scale = Affine(2.0, 0.0) Connects ports (connect) self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev) Exposes the ports the outside uses self.prev, self.next = self.scale.prev, self.shift.next

sequenceDiagram

    participant S as scale
    participant F as shift

    H->>S: run.write writes x
    F-->>H: values from older inputs (zeros at first)

In the with mujou.run(net) as run: block, the output right after a write is computed from older inputs, so wait for an output that meets the condition with wait_for, not read.

docs.title: 🧩 2. Write a Node
docs.text: This page writes Leaky, a leaky integrator whose state follows a differential equation, and runs two of them in a row. The rules every node keeps are in How Mujou Works.

docs.title: The node
docs.text:
Leaky follows its input \(u\) with the time constant \(\tau\). Its state \(x\) follows this differential equation.

\[ \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{u - x}{\tau} \] 
class Leaky(Node):
    """Follows its input ``u`` with the time constant ``tau`` (in seconds):

        dx/dt = (u - x) / tau

    ``on_update`` advances ``x`` by ``dt``, the time that passed since the last
    update, with the exact solution for an input held constant over the step:
    ``x`` moves the fraction ``1 - exp(-dt / tau)`` of the way to ``u``. That
    fraction stays below 1 for any ``dt``, so a long ``dt`` (a busy machine) never
    overshoots ``u``, and none of the elapsed time is lost.

    ``period`` is well below ``tau`` by default: a node downstream sees this
    output at most about one period late, a small delay next to ``tau``.
    """

    def __init__(self, tau: float, *, period: float = 0.001) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=period)
        self.tau = tau  # a setting, not state
        self.x = SCALAR.zeros()  # a tensor attribute: in the state by itself
        self.prev = Port(recv=SCALAR)
        self.next = Port(send=SCALAR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        u = self.prev.recv()
        self.x += (1 - math.exp(-dt / self.tau)) * (u - self.x)  # in place
        self.next.send(self.x)  # a copy: changing x later does not change it

docs.title: Update in proportion to dt
docs.text:
dt is not constant: it gets longer when the machine is busy (How Mujou Works), so always make the update proportional to dt.

Fixed step per update (avoid) time → Proportional to dt (write this) time → node A (loops fast) node B (loops slow) continuous-time solution AvoidWrite this 
# A fixed step per update: a node that loops faster changes faster
self.x += 0.001 * (u - self.x) / self.tau

# Cutting dt: the time cut off is lost, and the result drifts from the
# continuous-time solution (the exception is in "Stay stable for a long dt" below)
self.x += min(dt, 0.001) * (u - self.x) / self.tau

# Proportional to dt. For dx/dt = f(x), the simplest update is explicit Euler, x += dt * f(x)
self.x += dt * (u - self.x) / self.tau

docs.title: Stay stable for a long dt
docs.text:
When Way Example There is an exact solution Advance by dt with the exact solution Leaky (the equation below) There is no exact solution In one on_update, split dt into n steps no longer than a stable length, and update n times 4. Learn in a Node The instability comes from coupling with other nodes Cap the dt you use, at the cost of the time you drop. The values a node receives stay constant over dt, so splitting the step does not make it stable max_dt of the nodes of mujou.pc (TimeConstants) \[ x \leftarrow x + \left(1 - e^{-\Delta t / \tau}\right)(u - x) \]

Leaky updates with this equation. It is exact while \(u\) stays constant, and the coefficient \(1 - e^{-\Delta t / \tau}\) is below 1 for any dt, so \(x\) never overshoots \(u\).

docs.title: Adding noise
docs.text: To add noise to a continuous-time update, scale the change by dt and the standard deviation of the noise by \(\sqrt{dt}\), so that the result does not depend on how often the node updates.

docs.title: The state
docs.text:
Tensor attributes (self.x) join the state by themselves; settings from the arguments (self.tau) do not (what goes in the state).

AvoidWrite this 
# Assigns a new tensor: references held by an optimizer and the like still point at the old one
self.x = self.x + (1 - math.exp(-dt / self.tau)) * (u - self.x)

self.x += (1 - math.exp(-dt / self.tau)) * (u - self.x)  # in place (+=, copy_ and the like)

docs.title: The period
docs.text:
Case How to choose the period Keep the delay seen downstream (at most about one period) small Well below the time constant. Leaky defaults to 1 ms, below tau A chain fed by a node with a period (a sensor, say) The period downstream is no longer than the period of the input, since it reads the same input until the next arrives A node that must not wait period=0.0

A node with period=0.0 keeps a CPU core busy (Node).

docs.title: Two in a row
docs.text:
class LeakyChain(Network):
    """``u -> a -> b ->``: two leaky integrators with the time constant ``tau``."""

    def __init__(self, tau: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a = Leaky(tau)
        self.b = Leaky(tau)
        self.a.next.connect(self.b.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.a.prev, self.b.next
1 0 0 1τ 2τ 3τ 4τ 5τ time since the step → read 4 times, every τ/2 a: 1 − e^(−t/τ) b: 1 − e^(−t/τ)(1 + t/τ) The exact solution after the input steps from 0 to 1 at time 0 (step_response in leaky.py) 
if __name__ == "__main__":
    tau = 0.05
    net = LeakyChain(tau)
    with mujou.run(net) as run:
        # Step the input from 0 to 1 (write returns the time of the step), then
        # watch both integrators rise on the run's timer.
        start = run.write({net.prev: torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64)})
        for _ in range(4):
            run.timer.sleep(tau / 2)
            a, t_a = run.read_with_time(net.a.next)
            b, t_b = run.read_with_time(net.b.next)
            # Each output against the exact one at the time it was sent. On a busy
            # machine a node may not have sent since the step: its time is then
            # earlier than start, and the difference is negative (None, before
            # its first send, counts as long before the step).
            exact_a, _ = step_response(-math.inf if t_a is None else t_a - start, tau)
            _, exact_b = step_response(-math.inf if t_b is None else t_b - start, tau)
            print(
                f"a = {a.item():.3f} (exact {exact_a:.3f}), "
                f"b = {b.item():.3f} (exact {exact_b:.3f})"
            )
        # Hold the input for 10 time constants: both reach the equilibrium x = u.
        run.timer.sleep(10 * tau)
        b = run.read(net.next)
    print(f"after {10 * tau:.1f} s more: b = {b.item():.4f}")

uv run python examples/leaky.py

On a busy machine a node may not have sent anything since the step yet, and the difference between the time of the output and start is negative. Then the output is compared with 0, the exact solution before the step.

docs.title: 🧪 3. Test a Node
docs.text: This page tests Leaky from 2. Write a Node with mujou.run_manually. Such a run goes on a virtual time that moves only with step (two ways to run).

docs.title: The test
docs.text:
uv run pytest examples/test_leaky.py

class TestLeaky:
    def test_follows_the_exact_solution(self) -> None:
        tau, h, steps = 0.1, 0.001, 100
        node = Leaky(tau)
        one = torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64)
        expected = 0.0
        with mujou.run_manually(node, inputs={node.prev: one}) as run:
            for _ in range(steps):
                run.step(h)  # 1 ms later, then every node once (period is ignored)
                expected += (1 - math.exp(-h / tau)) * (1.0 - expected)
            y, t = run.read_with_time(node.next)
        assert t is not None and t.ns == steps * 1_000_000  # sent at the last step
        torch.testing.assert_close(y, torch.tensor(expected, dtype=torch.float64))

The output is compared with the exact solution computed with the same coefficient. No real time enters a manual run, so the time of the output is exactly steps milliseconds (t.ns == steps * 1_000_000).

When the reference does the same operations as the node in the same order, compare bit for bit with torch.equal instead of assert_close (the test in the next section).

docs.title: The order of the updates
docs.text:
class TestLeakyChain:
    def test_follows_the_discrete_algorithm(self) -> None:
        tau, h, steps = 0.01, 0.001, 50
        u = torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64)
        # The reference: the discrete algorithm, a then b at every step.
        a, b = SCALAR.zeros(), SCALAR.zeros()
        for _ in range(steps):
            a += (1 - math.exp(-h / tau)) * (u - a)
            b += (1 - math.exp(-h / tau)) * (a - b)  # b reads the new a

        net = LeakyChain(tau)
        with mujou.run_manually(net, inputs={net.prev: u}) as run:
            for _ in range(steps):
                run.step(h, net.a, net.b)  # a, then b, which reads a's new value
            y = run.read(net.next)
        assert torch.equal(y, b)  # the same operations: equal to the last bit

    def test_a_step_without_nodes_equals_the_order_from_the_output(self) -> None:
        tau, h, steps = 0.01, 0.001, 50
        u = torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64)
        by_order, at_once = LeakyChain(tau), LeakyChain(tau)
        with mujou.run_manually(by_order, inputs={by_order.prev: u}) as run:
            for _ in range(steps):
                run.step(h, by_order.b, by_order.a)  # b reads the old a
            expected = run.read(by_order.next)
        with mujou.run_manually(at_once, inputs={at_once.prev: u}) as run:
            for _ in range(steps):
                run.step(h)  # every node reads the values at the start of the step
            y = run.read(at_once.next)
        assert torch.equal(y, expected)

step(h, net.a, net.b) updates the nodes in the given order, so b reads what a sent in this step; with step(h) every node reads the values from the start of the step (two kinds of step).

docs.title: Save and restore
docs.text:
def run_steps(n: int, state: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Run a new ``LeakyChain`` for ``n`` steps of 1 ms and return its state."""
    net = LeakyChain(0.01)
    u = torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64)
    with mujou.run_manually(net, inputs={net.prev: u}, state=state) as run:
        for _ in range(n):
            run.step(0.001)
    return run.state_dict()


class TestRestore:
    def test_a_restored_run_goes_on_as_one_that_did_not_stop(self) -> None:
        straight = run_steps(20)
        # Ten steps, then ten more in a new instance restored from the first half,
        # on a VirtualTimer of its own that starts at the time of the state.
        resumed = run_steps(10, state=run_steps(10))
        x = resumed["nodes"]["b"]["state"]["x"]
        assert torch.equal(x, straight["nodes"]["b"]["state"]["x"])

A run that takes the state midway and goes on in a new instance matches a run that went on without stopping, to the last bit.

docs.text:
AvoidWrite this 
with mujou.run_manually(net) as run:
    with pytest.raises(NetworkError):
        run.step(0.001)  # a node raises ValueError here
# the shutdown at the end of the with block raises the same NetworkError again

from mujou import NetworkError

with pytest.raises(NetworkError) as info, mujou.run_manually(net) as run:
    run.step(0.001)  # a node raises ValueError here
assert isinstance(info.value.__cause__, ValueError)

Not only step but also the shutdown on leaving the with block raises NetworkError, so put pytest.raises in the same with statement as run_manually, around the whole block.

docs.text: This page writes a node that keeps learning, with backpropagation (BP, loss.backward()) inside itself, from a stream whose target changes while it runs. How far it learns is set by time, not by the number of batches. It builds on 2. Write a Node.

docs.title: The learner
docs.text:
class Learner(Node):
    """Follows the gradient flow dW/dt = -rate * dL/dW, learning once from each
    new batch for the time since the last one, and sends its loss on each batch
    before learning from it."""

    MAX_STEP = 0.01  # seconds: a longer explicit Euler step could diverge

    def __init__(self, rate: float) -> None:
        # Updating more often than the teacher sends would only re-read its batch.
        super().__init__(period=0.005, seed=0)
        self.rate = rate  # a setting, not state
        self.model = nn.Linear(1, 1)  # has state_dict: in the state by itself
        # seed reproduces only self.generator: initialize the module from it.
        nn.init.normal_(self.model.weight, std=0.1, generator=self.generator)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.model.bias)
        self.last = -1  # the time (ns) of the batch learned from last
        self.elapsed = 0.0  # seconds since then
        self.register_state("last")  # plain values that change: register them
        self.register_state("elapsed")
        self.prev = Port(recv=BATCH_SPEC)
        self.loss = Port(send=SCALAR, initial=torch.tensor(math.inf))  # no batch yet

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.elapsed += dt
        batch, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
        if t is None or t.ns == self.last:  # nothing sent yet, or nothing new
            return
        self.last = t.ns
        x, y = batch["x"], batch["y"]
        with torch.no_grad():  # the loss on an unseen batch needs no graph
            self.loss.send(nn.functional.mse_loss(self.model(x), y))
        # How far to learn is set by the time, not by the number of batches: move
        # by the elapsed time, in n equal steps no longer than MAX_STEP.
        n = max(1, math.ceil(self.elapsed / self.MAX_STEP))
        for _ in range(n):
            loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(self.model(x), y)  # records the graph
            loss.backward()
            with torch.no_grad():  # the step itself is not part of any graph
                for p in self.model.parameters():
                    assert p.grad is not None
                    p -= self.elapsed / n * self.rate * p.grad
                    p.grad = None
        self.elapsed = 0.0
How this example writes it Why More model and generator enter the state by themselves; last and elapsed are registered with register_state So that a resumed run continues learning where it left off Values of your own in the state The weights are initialized again from self.generator The default initialization of nn.Linear draws from the global generator every node shares, and does not reproduce Seeds and random numbers It compares the time from recv_with_time with the last one, and learns once from each new batch The learner runs faster than the teacher and reads the same batch more than once New value or re-read Gradients come from plain PyTorch, and the graph stays inside one update A graph that crosses nodes breaks locality Rules a node keeps 
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Teacher (every 10 ms)
    participant C as The learner's prev
    participant L as Learner (every 5 ms)
    L->>C: recv_with_time()
    C-->>L: initial value, time None → does not learn
    T->>C: send(batch 1)
    L->>C: recv_with_time()
    C-->>L: batch 1, time t1 → learns
    L->>C: recv_with_time()
    C-->>L: batch 1, time t1 (as before) → does not learn
    T->>C: send(batch 2)
    L->>C: recv_with_time()
    C-->>L: batch 2, time t2 → learns

docs.title: Learn by time
docs.text:
The learner does not take a fixed step per batch: it follows the gradient flow for the time elapsed since it last learned, so how far it learns depends on the time that passed, not on how often it runs (here rate = 5.0 and MAX_STEP = 0.01 s).

\[ \frac{dW}{dt} = -\text{rate}\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial W} \] elapsed = 25 ms (for example) step 1 ≈ 8.3 ms step 2 ≈ 8.3 ms step 3 ≈ 8.3 ms MAX_STEP = 10 ms n = ceil(25 / 10) = 3 Split into n = max(1, ceil(elapsed / MAX_STEP)) equal steps, each one step of explicit Euler

docs.title: The run
docs.text:
teacher, learner = Teacher(), Learner(rate=5.0)
teacher.next.connect(learner.prev)
net = mujou.Group(teacher=teacher, learner=learner)
with mujou.run(net, inputs={teacher.a: torch.tensor(A_BEFORE)}) as run:
    # How fast the learner learns depends on time, not on how often it runs:
    # follow its loss, giving each phase up to 5 s of real time.
    loss, t = run.wait_for(learner.loss, learned, timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None  # the loss on a batch, not the initial inf
    print(f"t = {float(t):.2f} s: loss = {loss.item():.6f}  (learned a = {A_BEFORE})")
    # The world changes: the same learner keeps learning, with no new phase.
    changed_at = run.write({teacher.a: torch.tensor(A_AFTER)})
    loss, t = run.wait_for(learner.loss, lambda loss: loss.item() > 1e-2, timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None
    print(
        f"t = {float(t):.2f} s: loss = {loss.item():.6f}  (a changed at {float(changed_at):.2f} s)"
    )
    loss, t = run.wait_for(learner.loss, learned, timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None
    print(f"t = {float(t):.2f} s: loss = {loss.item():.6f}  (learned a = {A_AFTER})")

# After the run, the nodes' attributes are the host's to read.
weight, bias = learner.model.weight.item(), learner.model.bias.item()
print(f"the learner's weight = {weight:.3f}, bias = {bias:.3f}")

The host follows the loss with wait_for and changes the target a midway with write. There is no mode to switch between learning and inference.

The number of torch's threads (here torch.set_num_threads(1)) is a setting of the whole process, so the host sets it before the run (Settings of the whole process).

docs.title: 🧠 5. Learn with PC-ALM
docs.text: mujou.pc splits a PyTorch model into nodes and learns it with PC-ALM (Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding, https://pub.sakana.ai/pc-alm/). Each node holds a part of the model and learns from its neighbors' messages only. This page learns a regression with pc.Chain. It builds on 4. Learn in a Node.

docs.title: The program
docs.text:
The chain learns \(y = \sin(2 x_1)\cos(x_2)\) from a stream of batches of 32 samples, and the loss before learning falls from about 0.4 to below 0.01.

docs.text:
SHOWN = 0.032  # seconds of the run's timer each batch is shown
# tau.h sets how fast the credit settles (and the period of the nodes, h / 2),
# and the weights learn once per batch, by SGD at the rate
# SHOWN / optimizer.tau = 0.3.
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3)
optimizer = pc.optim.SGD(tau=SHOWN / 0.3)
torch.manual_seed(0)  # the initial weights, before the run
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Linear(64, 1),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 2)),
    y=TensorSpec((B, 1)),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.loss.MSELoss(B),  # the loss of each sample, (B,)
    tau=tau,
    optimizer=optimizer,

)

docs.text:
torch.set_num_threads(1)
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)

losses: list[float] = []

        y = torch.sin(2 * x[:, :1]) * torch.cos(x[:, 1:])

            print(

    lam = run.state_dict()["nodes"]["layer0"]["state"]["lam"]
print(f"the mean |lam| of layer0 (its credit) at the end: {lam.abs().mean():.2e}")

docs.title: 💾 6. Save and Resume
docs.text: This page takes the state of a run, saves it to a file, and resumes from it in a new instance of the same network.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Run<br/>(running, or ended normally)"] -->|"run.state_dict()"| T["State tree<br/>(a plain dict on the CPU)"]
    T -->|"torch.save"| F[("File")]
    F -->|"torch.load"| T2["State tree"]
    T2 -->|"mujou.run(new instance, state=tree)"| B["Run that continues"]
"""Save the state of a run, and restore it in a new run that goes on from there.

A node collects its state by itself: every attribute that holds a
``torch.Tensor`` or an ``nn.Module``, and the state of its generator.
``Run.state_dict`` gathers the states of all nodes, the latest messages and the
time into one tree, a plain ``dict`` of CPU tensors. Save it with ``torch.save``
(or pickle), and read it back with ``torch.load``.
"""

import io
from typing import override

import torch
from torch import nn

import mujou
import mujou.time
from mujou import Node, Port, TensorSpec

VECTOR1 = TensorSpec((1,))


class Integrator(Node):
    """Integrates its input over time (dx/dt = u) and sends ``readout(x)``."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.x = VECTOR1.zeros()  # a tensor: part of the state
        self.readout = nn.Linear(1, 1)  # a module: part of the state
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR1)
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR1)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.x += dt * self.prev.recv()  # in place: other references to x stay valid
        with torch.no_grad():  # computed only to send: no graph
            self.next.send(self.readout(self.x))


class Model(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.integrator = Integrator()
        self.prev = self.integrator.prev
        self.next = self.integrator.next


one = torch.ones(1)

# Run for a while, then stop and take the state at the end.
net = Model()
with mujou.run(net, inputs={net.prev: one}) as run:
    run.timer.sleep(0.2)
tree = run.state_dict()  # after a normal end: the state at the stop
saved = tree["nodes"]["integrator"]["state"]  # this node's state_dict()
print("state of the node:", {k: type(v).__name__ for k, v in saved.items()})
file = io.BytesIO()  # or a path, such as "state.pt"
# Every tensor of the tree is on the CPU, so torch.load needs no GPU (a CUDA node's
# generator state still restores only into a CUDA node).
torch.save(tree, file)

# A new instance of the same network goes on from the saved state and time. A
# network runs once: run the one the tree came from again, and mujou.run raises.
restored = Model()
file.seek(0)
loaded = torch.load(file)  # the default weights_only=True reads the plain dict
with mujou.run(restored, inputs={restored.prev: one}, state=loaded) as run:
    # On a timer of its own that starts at the time of the tree: the global timer
    # and the other runs do not go back.
    assert run.timer is not mujou.time.global_timer
    print(f"restored at t = {float(run.timer.now()):.3f} s of its own timer")
    run.timer.sleep(0.1)
after = run.state_dict()["nodes"]["integrator"]["state"]

x0, x1 = saved["x"].item(), after["x"].item()
print(f"x = {x0:.3f} at the save, {x1:.3f} after 0.1 s more")
# The integral went on from the saved value: from 0, it would be about 0.1. (How
# far it gets in 0.2 s and 0.1 s depends on when the last update falls.)
assert x1 > x0 > 0
# The module was restored too: the new instance had other random weights.
assert torch.equal(after["readout"]["weight"], saved["readout"]["weight"])

The shape of the tree is in Run.state_dict. A network runs once, so the instance you took the tree from cannot resume; build a new instance of the same network (Rules a node keeps).

docs.title: The pause while taking it
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant R as Run
    participant N as Each node
    H->>R: run.state_dict()
    R->>N: asks to pause (the timer stops too)
    N->>N: finishes the current on_update
    N->>N: on_pause()
    R->>R: copies the state of every node (all of one time)
    N->>N: on_resume()
    R-->>H: the state tree
    Note over N: the paused time does not enter any dt afterwards

on_pause and on_resume let a node hold its I/O meanwhile. A run that ended with an exception has no state to take, so take it regularly during a long run (The state after an exception).

docs.title: When you resume
docs.text:
What to mind In the resumed run More The timer Runs on a timer of its own that starts at the tree's time The timer of a resumed run The network and its state Must have the paths, ports and connections, and the state keys and shapes, of the one the tree came from state of mujou.run Inputs inputs are written after the state and replace the tree's values inputs of mujou.run

Renaming an attribute changes a path

The paths of the nodes come from the attribute names, so a tree saved before a rename no longer resumes.

docs.title: Values of your own in the state
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["The value of a node's attribute"] --> Q1{"A tensor, or a mujou.Stateful<br/>(including nn.Module)?"}
    Q1 -- yes --> S["In the state by itself<br/>(so is the state of self.generator)"]
    Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Changes while the node runs?"}
    Q2 -- no --> C["A setting; not in the state"]
    Q2 -- yes --> Q3{"A type the default torch.load reads?"}
    Q3 -- yes --> R["Register it with register_state"]
    Q3 -- "no (a deque, ...)" --> O["Override state_dict and load_state_dict"]

A class of your own does not enter the state just by having state_dict and load_state_dict; inherit Stateful (the rules for registering a plain value are in register_state).

AvoidWrite 
class Counter:  # methods of the same names alone do not put it in the state
    def state_dict(self) -> dict[str, int]: ...
    def load_state_dict(self, state: Mapping[str, int]) -> None: ...

class Counter(mujou.Stateful):  # inherited: in the state by itself as an attribute
    def state_dict(self) -> dict[str, int]: ...
    def load_state_dict(self, state: Mapping[str, int]) -> None: ...

docs.title: Overriding state_dict and load_state_dict
docs.text:
state_dict returns super().state_dict() extended with your keys; load_state_dict passes super().load_state_dict the state without them, and keeps copies (clone) of the tree's tensors.

from collections import deque
from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any, override

import torch

from mujou import Node


class Recent(Node):
    """Keeps the last 8 inputs in a deque."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.recent: deque[torch.Tensor] = deque(maxlen=8)

    @override
    def state_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {**super().state_dict(), "recent": list(self.recent)}

    @override
    def load_state_dict(self, state: Mapping[str, Any]) -> None:
        self.recent = deque((x.clone() for x in state["recent"]), maxlen=8)  # a copy of the tree's
        super().load_state_dict({k: v for k, v in state.items() if k != "recent"})

docs.title: Files
docs.text: How you read it What it reads Note torch.load(f) (the default weights_only=True) A tree of tensors, numbers, strings, dicts, lists and tuples Does not read a tree holding objects of your own classes (from register_state or an override) torch.load(f, weights_only=False), pickle.load Objects of your own classes too Can run code from the file. Do not read files you do not trust

docs.title: Mujou
docs.text:
連続的継続学習のための非同期分散型深層学習フレームワーク

画像は、落合陽一の作品「リキッドユニバース」をもとに新たに制作したもの

mujou は、ノードをつないだネットワークで推論と学習を同時に行い続ける深層学習フレームワークである。

開発の初期段階

mujou はまだ開発の初期段階にある。API は予告なく変わることがある。

docs.title: 学び続けるネットワーク
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph T["従来の機械学習"]
        direction LR
        T1["学習（エポックを繰り返す）"] --> T2["重みを固定"] --> T3["推論"]
    end
    subgraph M["mujou"]
        direction LR
        M1["入力"] --> M2["ネットワーク（推論と学習を同時に）"] --> M3["出力"]
        M2 -->|"重みが変わり続ける"| M2
    end

名前は「諸行無常」の「無常」（常が無いこと）から取った。ストリームから学び続けて常に変わり続ける機械を作り、リアルタイム処理やロボティクスのように動きながら学ぶ用途を狙う。

次のプログラムでは、PC-ALM のノードの鎖（学ぶノードは 3 つ）が動き続けたまま、流れてくるバッチごとに、まずそのバッチを予測してからそのバッチで回帰を学ぶ（読み解きは 5. PC-ALM で学習する）。

SHOWN = 0.032  # seconds of the run's timer each batch is shown
# tau.h sets how fast the credit settles (and the period of the nodes, h / 2),
# and the weights learn once per batch, by SGD at the rate
# SHOWN / optimizer.tau = 0.3.
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=2e-3, r=4e-3)
optimizer = pc.optim.SGD(tau=SHOWN / 0.3)
torch.manual_seed(0)  # the initial weights, before the run
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Linear(64, 1),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 2)),
    y=TensorSpec((B, 1)),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.loss.MSELoss(B),  # the loss of each sample, (B,)
    tau=tau,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    learn_interval=0.75 * SHOWN,  # learn once, 3/4 of the way through each batch
)

torch.set_num_threads(1)
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
every = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)  # every sample has a target, and is new
losses: list[float] = []
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    for i in range(300):
        x = 2 * torch.rand(B, 2, generator=g) - 1
        y = torch.sin(2 * x[:, :1]) * torch.cos(x[:, 1:])
        sample = pc.msg.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=every, reset=every)
        p = pc.show(run, net, sample, seconds=SHOWN)
        losses.append(nn.functional.mse_loss(p["y_hat"], y).item())  # before learning
        if i == 0 or (i + 1) % 50 == 0:
            recent = losses[-50:]
            mean = sum(recent) / len(recent)
            print(
                f"batch {i + 1:3d}: loss {mean:.4f} (the mean of the last {len(recent)})"
            )
    # The state of a node, by its path: input, layer0, layer1, output.
    lam = run.state_dict()["nodes"]["layer0"]["state"]["lam"]
print(f"the mean |lam| of layer0 (its credit) at the end: {lam.abs().mean():.2e}")

docs.title: 特徴
docs.text:
• 🔄 推論と学習を同時に: 学習のモードも推論のモードも、エポックも無い
  • 🧩 PyTorch で書くノード: 各ノードは PyTorch で書き実行する
  • ⚡ 非同期のノード: 各ノードは自分の周期で更新し、ほかのノードを待たない
  • ⏱️ 連続時間: 実際に経った時間 dt に比例して更新する
  • 🧠 更新則は自由: ノードの中の BP、ノードをまたぐ PC-ALM、自作の則
  • 💾 状態を保存: ネットワークの状態を取得、後でその状態から再開
  • 🧪 シミュレーションと決定的なテスト: 仮想時間を手で進め、計算能力いっぱいでシミュレーション可能
